nodes.title: VideoNexus: Video Perception Beyond the Reasoning Context
nodes.authors: Yancheng Long, Xuanyu Zheng, Wei Chen, Luoyuan Zhang, Haoyang Xu, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao
nodes.summary: Understanding long videos requires locating evidence, resolving visual details, and integrating observations into an answer. Even when relevant evidence is present, performing these operations within long, dense visual sequences burdens both perception and reasoning. Video agents enable selective inspection, but returning frames to the planner still accumulates visual information in its reasoning context. Delegating perception reduces this burden, yet sparse sampling can miss decisive details, and per-frame descriptions can preserve context growth. We introduce VideoNexus, a training-free framework that separates detailed video perception from evidence-driven planning and reasoning. The planner controls where to inspect, what to resolve, and how densely to sample. Perception sub-agents process native audio-video in independent contexts and return compact, temporally grounded evidence for iterative search and verification. Using Gemini 3.8 Flash for both planning and perception, VideoNexus achieves 88.6% accuracy on full LVBench, exceeding same-backbone static ingestion and built-in agentic processing by 3.6 and 1.1 points, respectively, at 44% of the latter's measured API cost. A paired LVBench subset ablation shows lower planner input and higher accuracy. With Kimi K3 as the shared backbone, VideoNexus improves over the official Video-GAIA ReAct harness by 8.5 points in our evaluation. These results support compact evidence exchange for combining detailed observation with efficient planning and reasoning.
nodes.subject: End-to-End AD

nodes.title: Scribble Once, Segment the Sequence: Bidirectional Temporal Consistency for Weakly Supervised Segmentation in Echocardiography Sequences
nodes.authors: Vincent Li Weixin, Chen Jingkun, Vicente Grau
nodes.summary: Temporal medical image segmentation relies on pixel-wise annotations, which are prohibitively expensive for long image sequences. Existing weakly-supervised methods reduce the annotation burden per frame but still require repeated annotations across the sequence. Furthermore, sparse supervision can result in temporally unstable representations. Addressing both challenges requires a model that can leverage strong spatial priors from large-scale pretraining while minimizing reliance on dense annotations. Frozen 2D vision foundation models provide a promising basis for this by offering transferable spatial representations with low trainable parameters. However, their lack of explicit temporal modeling limits their ability to propagate reliable information across anatomical sequences. To address this, we present a weakly-supervised framework for temporal segmentation from a single scribble-annotated frame, with all remaining frames left unlabeled. The framework combines parameter-efficient adaptation of DINOv3 encoders present in the mean-teacher architecture. Furthermore, a set of complementary losses, including a temporal loss helps generate reliable segmentation priors for the unlabeled frames. This formulation decouples annotation costs from sequence length while retaining the transferable spatial knowledge of the pretrained encoder. Extensive experiments on the publicly available CAMUS and CardiacNet datasets demonstrate that our approach outperforms other scribble-supervised methods. These results show that accurate and temporally consistent segmentation can be achieved from extremely sparse supervision, substantially reducing annotation requirements for temporal echocardiographic segmentation and providing a practical framework for scalable clinical deployment.
nodes.subject: End-to-End AD

nodes.title: Region-VAD: Video Anomaly Localization and Detection via Region Selection
nodes.authors: Giacomo D'Amicantonio
nodes.summary: Anomalies are local events, yet weakly supervised video anomaly detection scores them globally. Most methods pool an entire frame into a single vector, rank frames by that vector, and derive a location afterwards as a saliency map of the score. Full-frame pooling mixes the anomaly with its background, so a detector can reach competitive benchmark scores from scene context without being able to show where in the scene the anomaly occurs. We introduce Region-VAD, which first selects a region and then detects the anomaly from that region alone. Region-VAD selects an explicit rectangle over the tokens of a frozen foundation model and scores anomalousness only from the tokens inside the box, through attention pooling followed by a standard temporal head. The rectangle is not learned, it is the box in which the frozen tokens change most between consecutive segments, in all four feature projections of the encoder, and it is found by exhaustive search over the rectangles of the token grid. Only the pooling and the temporal head are trained, from video-level labels without boxes, masks or frame-level annotations, and no trained component reads a token outside the selected region. Experiments on five datasets, with one localizer configuration shared by all datasets and backbones, show that Region-VAD achieves state-of-the-art anomaly localization on UCF-Crime and MSAD at competitive detection performance.
nodes.subject: End-to-End AD

nodes.title: CivilBench: Benchmarking Vision-Language Models for Multimodal Information Integration in Civil Engineering
nodes.authors: Dan Yuan, Yue Wen, Zhili He, Zhenkui Zhou, Shicen Liu, Ziqiang Zheng
nodes.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), is increasingly applied in civil and structural engineering for disaster assessment, structural analysis, and engineering decision support. However, the extent to which current VLMs possess the reasoning capabilities required for reliable engineering judgments remains unclear. In this work, we introduce CivilBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating VLMs in civil engineering and disaster-related scenarios. CivilBench covers three major task families: Sequential Reasoning, Image-based Structural Understanding, and Open-world Understanding, encompassing numerical reasoning, structural damage assessment, risk inference, causal analysis, and repair planning. The benchmark is constructed through a systematic pipeline of domain-specific data collection, engineering-oriented captioning, expert annotation, question design, and quality verification. Evaluation of representative state-of-the-art VLMs reveals substantial limitations in domain-specific reasoning, with Sequential Reasoning emerging as a major bottleneck, particularly when models must infer numerical relationships from sparse structured observations. Further experiments show that numerical priors and external knowledge can alleviate these limitations, although their effectiveness depends on the model's ability to reliably interpret and use the available evidence. CivilBench provides a capability-oriented testbed for identifying reasoning limitations and evaluating progress toward reliable AI-assisted engineering decision-making. The benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/traceuryuan/CivilBench.
nodes.subject: End-to-End AD

nodes.title: Sparse Attention for Visual Generation: Toward Algorithm-System Co-Design
nodes.authors: Majun Zhang, Yuan Guo, Decheng Wu, Jiayang Xu, Changhao Pan, Fan Zhuo, Xiaoda Yang, Chenyuhao Wen, Zhou Zhao
nodes.summary: Rapid advances in image and video generation have enabled high-fidelity synthesis at higher resolutions and longer durations, making the quadratic cost of dense self-attention a major bottleneck as visual token sequences grow. Sparse attention seeks to preserve generation quality at lower computational cost by retaining informative query-key interactions and omitting less consequential ones, with end-to-end gains depending on the cost of constructing sparse support and the efficiency with which the system maps the resulting workload to hardware. We survey sparse attention for visual generation through a 4+1+3 analytical framework that links algorithmic design to system implementation. The framework examines how static and dynamic methods use source information and the evidence derived from it to decide which interactions to retain and at what granularity, while accounting for the roles of reuse in reducing repeated computation and correction in compensating for omitted contributions. We relate these algorithmic choices to their implementation on hardware through the framework's three system dimensions of data organization, execution, and dataflow. We summarize common evaluation metrics and discuss open challenges and research directions, providing researchers and practitioners with a reference for the joint design of sparse attention algorithms and systems.
nodes.subject: End-to-End AD

nodes.title: MedJev: A System One Vision-Language Decision Model for Fast and Effective Medical Image Understanding
nodes.authors: Fan Zhang, Hao Wu, Jinyang Wu, Hongyu Qu, Zheng Lian, Dongfu Yin, Qingsong Wen, Pheng-Ann Heng
nodes.summary: Medical image understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) typically relies on autoregressively generating reasoning and answer tokens. These unnecessary tokens make the inference cost scale with the response length and force the answer to be parsed from free-form text, incurring avoidable latency and decision errors. To this end, we introduce \textsc{MedJev}, a \emph{system one} vision-language decision model that maps medical images, questions, and candidate answers directly to decisions in a single multimodal forward pass, without any autoregressive generation process. For fast inference, \textsc{MedJev} removes the upper language layers and the generative output pathway, while keeping the full vision pathway and all visual tokens. On this shortened backbone, a decision head scores each candidate by pretrained query--key matching and refines the scores with a lightweight multilayer perceptron (MLP) residual, coupling the pretrained matching structure with task-specific nonlinear discrimination. Built on Qwen3.5-4B, \textsc{MedJev}-4B improves both accuracy and speed over the original model on each of four medical image classification and visual question answering benchmarks, with an absolute accuracy gain of \textbf{7.93\%} and a \textbf{6.04$\times$} end-to-end speedup. Further comparison with 20 cutting-edge models shows that \textsc{MedJev}-4B achieves state-of-the-art performance and inference speed among 4B--9B general and medical VLMs, indicating that direct multimodal decision making is an effective route to fast and effective medical image understanding.
nodes.subject: End-to-End AD

nodes.title: Interpretable deep concepts of organoid morphology
nodes.authors: Lion Jasper Gleiter, Tingying Peng
nodes.summary: Image-based classification of organoid morphologies can indicate drug response, viability, or successful differentiation. In recent work, learned representations outperform handcrafted features as the basis for downstream classifiers. However, their black-box nature hides the morphological cues a classifier relies on. Based on the foundation models DINOv3 (general-purpose) and ViTAMIn-O (organoid-specific), we train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to learn interpretable concepts related to distinct organoid morphologies. We annotate concepts with spatial labels (organoid, organoid wall, background) and compute their dataset specificity and task relevance across five tasks. The spatial labels of DINOv3 concepts yield coarse organoid segmentations on out-of-domain datasets. Filtering concepts by spatial label in the DINOv3-SAE improves downstream AUROC for three of the five tasks. Qualitative analysis of the most relevant concepts further reveals a confounding factor introduced by our preprocessing in one task. Through such insights, interpretable concepts could help improve the reliability of classifiers and guide the future development of organoid representation models. The trained SAEs will be made available upon publication.
nodes.subject: End-to-End AD

nodes.title: QASK-Edit: Adaptive Sparse Attention Across Queries and Key Sources for Efficient Video Editing
nodes.authors: Hengrui Liu, Wenbo Xu, Ziqi Sheng, Wei lu
nodes.summary: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have achieved strong performance in generation based video editing, but suffer from high inference latency due to the long token sequences formed by conditioning inputs and generated videos. Although training-free sparse attention reduces this cost, existing methods typically apply a fixed retention ratio or a single threshold shared across all tokens. In this work, we view video editing as conditional generation and identify a key insight: attention demand varies significantly both across different key sources (e.g., source videos, reference images, audio, text, and generated videos) and across queries within each source. Motivated by this, we propose QASK-Edit (Query-Adaptive Sparsity over Key Sources for Video Editing), a training-free sparse attention framework that allocates computation independently for each query and key source. Specifically, for each query, QASK-Edit considers both the attention mass and approximation risk of each block. It then evaluates candidate routing thresholds against each key source's risk budget, choosing exact computation or approximations to dynamically adjust sparsity for each query. Extensive experiments on three video editing models demonstrate that QASK-Edit achieves up to $1.46\times$ end-to-end speedup over dense attention pipeline while preserving both editing quality and unedited region fidelity. Furthermore, QASK-Edit generalizes directly to Reference-to-Video generation, delivering up to $1.36\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality.
nodes.subject: End-to-End AD

nodes.title: Latent Lattice Language Models
nodes.authors: Shivam Duggal, Zongze Wu, William T. Freeman, Antonio Torralba, Richard Zhang, Eli Shechtman
nodes.summary: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN-Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4x larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: ViRA: Toward Ultra-High-Resolution Visual Agents via Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization
nodes.authors: Huawei Lin, Jinting Liu, Tongyan Wang, Xuyang Chen, Ruihua Shi, Zhichao Xu, Jiaxin Qin, Guoshenghui Zhao, Baijian Yang, Yingjie Victor Chen, Tan Yu, Weijie Zhao
nodes.summary: Visual agents answer questions about ultra-high-resolution photos by zooming into the relevant regions. However, existing agents often answer from common sense instead of reading the evidence. Reinforcement learning (RL) on the final answer cannot correct this, because a guess earns the same reward as reading. We propose Cross-Input Relative Policy Optimization (CrossRPO), which trains agents on contrast sets. A contrast set asks one question about several versions of an image that differ only in a small region with the evidence and have different answers, so only reading the evidence solves the whole set. CrossRPO rewards solving the whole set, and we prove that it does not reinforce a set answered from common sense. We build contrast sets for training (ViRA-Train) and evaluation (ViRA-Bench) by editing one small object in images of 21 to 120 megapixels, and we photograph further sets with real changes (ViRA-Bench-Real) to exclude editing traces. We train two Visual Reasoning Agents, ViRA-9B and ViRA-27B, with CrossRPO on only about 3,500 items of ViRA-Train each. CrossRPO achieves 63.3% set accuracy on ViRA-Bench at the maximum resolution, against 59.3% for GRPO. ViRA-9B is the most accurate open model of its size on all benchmarks, and ViRA-27B outperforms Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6-Luna, both at their highest thinking level, on most benchmarks.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: Quantifying the added value of human forecaster discussions for tropical cyclone intensity prediction
nodes.authors: Ilia Azizi, Frederick Iat-Hin Tam, Marc-Olivier Boldi, Valérie Chavez-Demoulin, Tom Beucler
nodes.summary: The National Hurricane Center routinely releases Tropical Cyclone Discussions that offer insights into its tropical cyclone forecasts. This study examines the added value of these discussions for intensity forecasting beyond a set of numerical predictors. For 637 Atlantic and eastern North Pacific tropical cyclones from the 2002-2023 hurricane seasons, we analyze the discussion text and its combination with 13 hurricane environmental predictors from SHIPS and ERA5 10-meter wind fields, for forecasting intensity changes at lead times of 24 to 120 hours using three modeling methods. In one approach, an end-to-end deep learning framework for the text shows that the discussions alone offer comparable value for 24-hour intensity forecasts to the SHIPS predictors. Adding discussion information to the SHIPS predictors in an ensemble of five such models reduces the mean absolute error of 24-hour maximum sustained wind forecasts for 2022-2023 cyclones from 9.89 to 8.90 kt, with a confidence interval that excludes zero when whole storms are resampled. The ERA5 wind fields have a minor effect on mean absolute error in wind predictions, and model rankings differ across predicted variables, lead times and model types. We provide prediction intervals for these forecasts, whose coverage falls below the 90% target during rapid intensification. Analysis of the text shows that words related to intensity and intensity change (such as intensify, weaken, eyewall and category) are important for the model predictions. This retrospective study shows the added value of the forecasters' discussions and suggests that multi-modal learning can help understand the predictive contribution of expert human judgment. The reanalysis data differ from real-time analyses, and the discussions are issued at least three hours after the valid time of the other inputs, so these results should not be interpreted operationally.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting with Physics-Indexed Specialist Memory: the Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent
nodes.authors: Blas Eugenio Vicco Zarate, Miguel Hernán Vicco
nodes.summary: Continual reinforcement learning requires adaptation to changing conditions while preserving performance under previously encountered dynamics. It was investigated whether specialists generated by evolutionary search can provide a reusable memory when combined with environment detection and failure-driven search. The Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent (ENA) evolves small neural networks without gradients, archives selected policies by detected dynamic regime, and retrieves them through Bayesian policy reuse. The architecture was evaluated in non-stationary CartPole and HalfCheetah environments. In the 30-replicate CartPole ablation, the complete architecture achieved a mean success rate of 83.2% across the five test environments. Among variants that learned the harder CartPole environments, the complete architecture showed the most consistent retention. A selection ablation also showed that the retrieval rule affected performance. In the evaluated sequences, ENA adapted more slowly than PPO on CartPole and achieved lower returns than SAC on HalfCheetah. The evidence concerns the complete architecture and does not isolate gradient-free optimization as the cause of retention or establish superiority over other continual-learning methods.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: Surrogate-Assisted Compact-Model Extraction for SKY130 CMOS at 77 K
nodes.authors: Aaron Wang, Olivia Gzamouranis, Vaibhav Lohia, Hershel Fei Xun Weiner, Olivia Seidel, Richard Cavanaugh, Giuseppe Di Guglielmo, Nhan Tran, Davide Braga
nodes.summary: Cryogenic circuit design requires compact transistor models that reproduce measured low-temperature behavior and run in standard circuit simulators. We fit BSIM4 parameters to measured I-V curves of SkyWater 130 nm (SKY130) transistors at 77 K using a neural surrogate of NGSpice. The surrogate maps compact-model parameters and device geometry to the complete set of output and transfer characteristics. Extraction is a bounded least-squares search: a bank of NGSpice simulations supplies initial candidates, finite differences of the surrogate supply the local Jacobian, and NGSpice re-simulates the resulting cards before selection. On 18 measured geometries, we compare a search over seven card parameters with a search over 43 parameters selected by NGSpice sensitivity. Relative to NGSpice re-simulations of the previously released cards, the two searches reduce the in-sample mean relative root-mean-square error (RRMS) by 17% and 26%, respectively. The 43-parameter search has the lower overall error, but the seven-parameter search has the lower mean on high-bias curves, and some individual curves have higher error than with the released cards under both searches.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: CertiSum: Bitwise-Identical MXFP4 Training Across Platforms and Parallelism Layouts
nodes.authors: Steve Rhyner, Yubo Gao, Stefan de Lasa, Sankeerth Durvasula, Nandita Vijaykumar
nodes.summary: Training with MXFP4, a 4-bit microscaling format, is non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different results across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors. These differences complicate debugging and training audits and can cause training and inference engines to disagree. We present CertiSum to make MXFP4 training bitwise invariant across runs, parallelism layouts, and GPU vendors. Its key insight is that native FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is often already exact for every summation order. CertiSum collects statistics during quantization to certify native matrix multiplication results, recomputes uncertified outputs exactly, and uses exact kernels directly where certification rarely succeeds. CertiSum keeps quantization blocks unchanged across layouts and merges partial sums without rounding, including in attention and weight-gradient computation. In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, CertiSum preserves training states bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across changes in data, tensor, and context parallelism on MI350X. Across three 8B--14B models on FineWeb-Edu using MI350X, it adds 11.8--60.5% to training-step latency relative to its non-exact MXFP4 counterpart at the larger evaluated input shapes, with speedups of up to $1.24\times$ over BF16 and $1.70\times$ over deterministic BF16.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: When Tool Names Are Not Identities: Measuring Provider Misbinding in MCP-Based AI Agents
nodes.authors: Zeynab Anbiaee, Sajjad Dadkhah, Ali A. Ghorbani
nodes.summary: Large language model (LLM) applications increasingly act as agents that select and invoke external tools. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes this interaction by allowing clients to compose tools advertised by multiple servers. However, tool metadata used for discovery and selection is not, by itself, necessarily bound to a verified provider identity. This paper studies this gap as tool-provider misbinding: a failure in which a request intended for a legitimate provider is instead resolved to an attacker-controlled tool. The attacker does not compromise the host, LLM, legitimate server, or network channel; it only operates another MCP server that advertises tools with chosen metadata. We formulate tool provider misbinding as an attacker-controlled tool-selection optimization problem and evaluate it in a controlled MCP environment across five LLM-based clients. The results show that interactions drive misbinding. The strongest failures occur when exact-name collision, task-aligned description, and compatible schema reinforce one another, but authority-enhanced descriptions with compatible schema can also cause wrong-provider execution or unresolved provider ambiguity without name collision. Different models expose the same provider-binding weakness differently, including attacker-controlled provider selection, clarification requests, and unstable or inconsistent provider resolution.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: DynSurvX: Time-Resolved Explanations for Dynamic Survival Predictions
nodes.authors: Van Tuan Nguyen, Agathe Guilloux
nodes.summary: Recent survival models integrating longitudinal data achieve strong predictive performance, but their predictions are often difficult to interpret, limiting their clinical use. We propose DynSurvX, a model-agnostic explainability framework for dynamic survival prediction with mixed static and longitudinal covariates. Based on Shapley values, DynSurvX introduces a hierarchical two-phase strategy that first identifies influential longitudinal features and then adaptively refines their temporal importance, enabling fine-grained explanations while reducing computational cost. The framework provides time-resolved explanations that evolve as new patient data become available. Experiments on simulated and two clinical datasets show varying agreement with theoretical importance across prediction models, with closer agreement for better-performing models, alongside clinically interpretable insights in real-world settings. It remains robust across prediction settings and reduces computation time by 41--80\% relative to the temporal explanation baseline, making dynamic explanations practical.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: Severe but Harmless: Stress-Testing Shift Severity for Frozen Time-Series Forecasters
nodes.authors: Korede R. Bishi, Dominic Okonkwo, Adetayo Okunoye
nodes.summary: Zero-shot time-series foundation models (TSFMs) have become attractive alternatives to task-specific models because they handle diverse downstream tasks, including anomaly detection and forecasting, without per-series training. However, time-series data undergo distribution shifts, and the dissimilarity between two regimes is commonly scored with statistical measures such as Wasserstein-1, where a higher score is read as a more severe shift. In systematic experiments using three established severity measures on nine regime shifts from three standard traffic datasets, we show that these measures do not reliably predict degradation for instance-normalized TSFMs. The regimes rated most severe are not the regimes that degrade the models most, and degradation reaches 29% in the lowest-scoring regime. In most cases, the audit shows no positive relationship between measured severity and model degradation. We provide an equivariance-based stress-testing analysis that explains why severity readings can become decoupled from model degradation.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: Reading or Remembering? Measuring Temporal Contamination in Language Models
nodes.authors: Arunkumar V, Gangadharan G. R., S. Senthilkumar
nodes.summary: Language models are now used to read central-bank text for economic forecasting, but most were trained on text written after the documents they read. A model reading a 2021 FOMC statement may already know that inflation rose in 2022, so part of its apparent skill can be memory of the outcome, a temporal form of test-set contamination. We measure this memory on FOMC statements and minutes from 2000 to 2026 by comparing modern open models with chronologically consistent models, which are trained only on text from before a fixed date. Asked about past GDP outcomes given only a date, models that cannot know the answer still reach an AUC of up to 0.64 from priors on dates and eras, so chance is the wrong baseline. Against these memory-free models on the same questions, most modern models recall which years had strong growth. Membership-inference scores sort documents by era and document type rather than by whether a model saw them, as exact counts in an open pretraining corpus show. In real-time nowcasts, every lookahead premium we estimate on US GDP is smaller than the forecast comparison can detect at macroeconomic sample sizes, and none on GDP or inflation survives correction for multiple testing. Lookahead audits should therefore measure memory directly against memory-free models on the same items.

nodes.title: Benchmarking memory and nonlinear processing capacity of quantum recurrent neural networks for time series prediction
nodes.authors: José Daniel Viqueira, Andrés Gómez, David Mera
nodes.summary: Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising approach to time series prediction. While quantum reservoir computing has been widely explored for this setting, variational quantum models tailored to sequential data remain comparatively understudied, largely because they are difficult to train. In this work, we present a rigorous benchmark of variational quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) on time series prediction tasks, focusing on two key capabilities: memory and nonlinear processing. We introduce a task-driven methodology that quantifies model capacity, enabling an intuitive and fair comparison across architectures, including classical recurrent baselines. We evaluate the proposed framework on two generic benchmark tasks and on a synthetic dataset describing a chaotic system. Overall, the quantum models achieve performance comparable to their classical counterparts, but classical models scale better with the memory size within the range studied. Notably, one QRNN variant shows higher average capacity on the task designed to jointly probe memory and nonlinear capacity. Moreover, our results show that quantum models offer better capacity when we are able to find a good parameter initialization. However, the increasing sensitivity to initialization leads to a lower probability of finding good solutions as the model size increases. These results provide a principled starting point for designing richer quantum recurrent architectures and for assessing where they may offer practical benefits.

nodes.title: ONAM: Fitting Orthogonal Neural Additive Models for Post-Hoc Interpretability of Black-Box Predictions
nodes.authors: David Köhler, Matthias Schmid
nodes.summary: Modern machine learning models, such as artificial neural networks, achieve high predictive performance through increasingly complex black-box architectures, limiting their use in settings where transparency, interpretability, and fairness are required. Here we present the R package ONAM, which provides a novel and practical implementation of functional decomposition, a technique to facilitate the interpretability of black-box models through structured effect representations. ONAM implements an algorithmic framework for the post-hoc decomposition of predictions into components associated with different input features. The package is designed for usability and efficiency, including functionalities for visualization as well as quantitative measures to assess interpretability. As a model-agnostic method, it can be applied to a wide range of prediction models. We describe the mathematical foundations, algorithmic design, and software architecture of ONAM. A central result of the proposed methodology is that the resulting decomposition satisfies the condition of hierarchical orthogonality, thereby guaranteeing that all components are identifiable and uniquely defined.

nodes.title: TRACE: Topological Representations for Anomaly detection through Contrastive Embeddings
nodes.authors: Sydney Johns
nodes.summary: Intrusion detectors must recognize evolving malicious behavior even when confirmed attack labels are scarce or incomplete. We present TRACE, a topology-aware graph contrastive learning framework for label-efficient intrusion detection. TRACE learns from benign system-activity graphs by combining message-passing and topological representations, then assigns anomaly scores in the same projected embedding space optimized by the contrastive objective. This design captures both local interactions and graph-scale structural deviations without using attack labels during representation learning. A labeled validation set containing benign and malicious graphs is used only to calibrate the anomaly threshold. We evaluate TRACE on StreamSpot, GraSec-IoT, and Unicorn Wget against a supervised graph neural network and the benign-only GraphCL baseline. TRACE obtains F1 scores of 0.923, 0.790, and 0.583, respectively. Compared with GraphCL, this is higher on StreamSpot (0.450) and Unicorn Wget (0.203), but lower on GraSec-IoT (0.975). The supervised model leads on StreamSpot and GraSec-IoT, whereas TRACE has the highest F1 on Unicorn Wget. The mixed results show that topology-aware benign-only learning can improve detection in some graph settings but does not provide a uniform advantage.

nodes.title: Right Reason, Wrong Advice: Evaluating Recourse in LLM Explanations of Denied Requests
nodes.authors: Arunkumar V
nodes.summary: Language models increasingly write the explanations people receive when a rule system denies their request. If several rules deny the request independently, an explanation can name a true reason and still leave the person denied after they fix it. We call the missing property recourse validity: changing what the explanation cites, without changing what was asked for, can flip the decision. We compute it exactly, and a hitting-set argument predicts from the policy alone when a correct reason fails. In six of seven rule systems ported from access control and US benefit eligibility, a single correct reason almost never gives recourse when several reasons apply. Across 20 LLMs, checks of whether the cited reasons are correct, computed or asked of an LLM judge, are close to chance at spotting this failure, as the argument predicts. A strong judge asked whether acting on the explanation would work does spot it. Stronger and reasoning models do better but still fail on many denials with four or more independent reasons. Asking for every rule helps every open model with room to improve. Explanations of eligibility decisions should be built from the decision function and judged by whether acting on them works.

nodes.title: The cost of enforcing long-run coverage: a phase transition in online conformal prediction
nodes.authors: Yu Gui, Rina Foygel Barber, Cong Ma
nodes.summary:
Consider an online prediction setting, where at each time, we are given a new feature vector and asked to provide a prediction interval or prediction set that will likely contain the corresponding response. In this setting, if the data points are i.i.d. (or more generally, exchangeable), conformal prediction provides a mechanism for building valid prediction sets around the output of any trained model, offering coverage probability $\geq 1-α$ at each time $t$. In practice, however, issues such as distribution drift, changepoints, or other challenges may cause violations of the i.i.d. assumption. In this adversarial setting, online conformal prediction methods can still offer guarantees on long-run empirical coverage. However, there is a trade-off between these two types of goals: enforcing tight constraints on long-run empirical coverage to protect against the adversarial setting can lead to unstable oscillations in the instantaneous training-conditional coverage in the i.i.d. setting.
  In this work, we seek best-of-both-worlds algorithms that aim to minimize cumulative error in instantaneous training-conditional coverage when in the i.i.d. setting, while also offering long-run empirical coverage guarantees in the adversarial setting. Specifically, consider a condition that requires long-run empirical coverage to deviate from the target level $1-α$ by at most $\mathcal{O}(T^{-β})$, for some $β\in[0,1]$. We prove that this family of conditions can be described with a phase transition. For $β\in[0,\frac{1}{2}]$, it is possible to construct algorithms satisfying such a constraint in the adversarial setting, while offering the same instantaneous coverage performance as split conformal prediction if the data is in fact i.i.d. On the other hand, for $β\in(\frac{1}{2},1]$, this type of condition comes at a cost, and does not achieve best-of-both-worlds behavior.

nodes.title: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents
nodes.authors: Brian T. Weston, Alondra Torres Contreras, Aldair E. Gongora
nodes.summary: We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator. An agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth. On a held-out split (93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes), models handle procedural traps. When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating they are 95% sure: their ranges contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, against 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort the failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose the missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes, against 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss; Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating, which keeps Astra calibrated even when it does not name the cause. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold, replicated on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. A pre-registered effort ablation shows that the correction is latent in the Claude 5.5 models: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but only with 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 is the most accurate model at default effort (interval score 1.9 times better than Astra's) but writes 6 times as many tokens, and at Astra's token count it falls short. We release the environment, graders and harness.

nodes.title: Seen but Unsaid: Locating and Repairing Cross-Image Comparison in Vision-Language Models
nodes.authors: Zhaoning Zhang
nodes.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the answer can be decoded from their own hidden states. We trace this failure from the visual tokens to the answer letter, in Qwen3-VL (2B-32B), InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B, on synthetic shape matching, same-instance point correspondence (HPatches), and semantic correspondence (SPair-71k), and find two distinct failure points, a small set of attention heads that carries the comparison, and a repair that touches 0.02% of the parameters. Two failure points: exact copies are compared but not read out. An answer-position probe exceeds the calibrated output by 15 to 25 points in every family, for nameable and unnameable shapes alike, and steering along the probe's direction moves no more answers than random directions. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but never reach the answer. One pathway: redistributing the cross-image attention of 16-32 heads, with its mass preserved, removes 17-22 points of synthetic and 15-32 points of HPatches accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads. A lever that training finds on its own: training only these heads' query and key projections raises SPair-71k accuracy by 28.3 points (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 25.1 points (InternVL3.5-8B), beats both layer-matched and attention-matched heads, and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. An unconstrained all-layer adapter routes 21-51% of its gain through the attention of the same heads, against at most 7% for random heads, and does so by changing what they read (83-86% of the effect) rather than their weights. Every decision rule was frozen before its run, and every reported number is recomputed by independent verification scripts.

nodes.title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle
nodes.authors: Arunkumar V, Manoranjan Gandhudi, Gangadharan G. R., Arun Prakash, S. Senthilkumar
nodes.summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding: the sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. A model-free audit of the verifier, its selection error and gap sign, together with a short saturation pilot, anticipates which phenotype a run will produce. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the phenotypes recur, sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps remain the steeper branch. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles.

nodes.title: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier
nodes.authors: Arunkumar V, Manoranjan Gandhudi, Gangadharan G. R., Arun Prakash, S. Senthilkumar
nodes.summary: When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more. For an executable policy over an enumerable context space this minimal sufficient reason can be computed exactly, so an explanation is scored against ground truth rather than a proxy for it. We use that exactness to ask what a model can learn from a verifier that has no error in it. The explainer sees one request and one decision, never the policy, and has thirty turns in which it may call the policy on altered requests and ask whether a candidate set of facts is sufficient. Frontier models find the exact reason about half the time with the tools alone, and one sentence telling them to shrink the answer lifts Haiku 4.5 from 58% to 75%. A 4B model fine-tuned on 2000 traces of the deletion algorithm reaches 92% on the policy it was trained on. Teacher kind is what moves this: at matched data size the algorithm-taught student leads the frontier-taught one in all three training seeds, and the two arms never overlap. What the student learns is a fixed schedule of sufficiency checks, and the schedule does not travel. On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Reinforcement learning from the exact reward leaves held-out accuracy where it was and inverts the strategy, from probing the policy to spending the entire budget on sufficiency checks. The oracle made the effect of training legible, but it did not make training better.

nodes.title: Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety
nodes.authors: Charles Xiao
nodes.summary: When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source, so text-similarity guardrails that attempt to flag the former risk conflating these two cases. We test this distinction using DonkeyRail, a public classifier combining BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR features, deployed in a controlled three-agent email relay, defining a behavioral measure in which an output counts as functional (the injected procedure induces fresh computations in two subsequent agents) independent of the detector's score, alongside legitimate controls that explicitly authorize quotation and reuse. At its default threshold the classifier misses 8 of 19 functional outputs while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies, with every completed quotation and template-reuse reply triggering a false alert; calibrating for low false positives on one template set does not transfer, as the recalibrated threshold detects only one functional output and still produces 15 false alerts on new templates. We also identify an operating-point error in all 21 published classifier configurations, where ROC interpolation replaces direct threshold application, and show formally that high AUC against a surface-level text criterion provides no distribution-free guarantee of high AUC against the behavioral target, while the existing evaluation labels lack the joint observations needed to estimate the gap. An authorization analysis further shows that identical visible transcripts can require different safety decisions depending on the governing policy, a distinction no observation-only classifier can resolve. These results argue for behavioral and policy-grounded evaluation over text-similarity guardrails.

nodes.title: Almost Controlled: The FDR of Benjamini-Hochberg on Weighted Conformal p-Values
nodes.authors: Ryan Lim
nodes.summary: Weighted conformal p-values generalize conformal inference to cases with covariate shift. One way to use them is to pass them to the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure, either to decide which test units to select or to detect outliers. But weighted conformal p-values may not be positively dependent, so we want to know: does BH still control the false discovery rate (FDR) in finite samples? Based on experiments, it appears to, but we prove it doesn't. We give two counterexamples, certified in exact rational arithmetic, where the FDR exceeds its target level $q$. We also identify how large the difference between the FDR and $q$ can be. With $n$ calibration points, $m$ test units and weight ratio $B$, the relative excess $\mathrm{FDR}/q-1$ is bounded by a function of $n$, $m$, $B$ and $q$ that is of order $\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ when $Bm/(nq)$ is small. The bound holds for every configuration with $B\le n$ and every $n$. This order can be reached when multiple non-null test units share a common threshold: in a Poisson-limit model, that configuration's excess is $c(q)\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ to first order as $B/n\to0$ and then $m\to\infty$. For some fixed distributions with this structure, the excess decreases only like $n^{-1/2}$ as $n$ grows. If every test unit is null, the excess is $O(B/n)$ at fixed $m$, and in certain configurations it grows linearly with $m$. To assist practitioners in judging how large the FDR can be, we turn that bound, which depends only on $n$, $m$, $q$ and $B$, into a lowered BH level with proved finite-sample control, and give a much less conservative rule of thumb that covers every worst case we were able to find but provides no guarantee.

nodes.title: Leverage-Enhanced Sampling Owen Method for Explainable Artificial Intelligence
nodes.authors: Jing Liu, Elena Parilina, Chi Zhao
nodes.summary: Recently, the Shapley value has been widely applied in machine learning for feature importance analysis and model explainability. The multilinear extension of games proposed by Owen (1972) expresses the Shapley value as the integral of partial derivatives along the main diagonal of the cube. Direct evaluation of this integral requires exponential-time computation of the partial derivatives. To improve computational efficiency, we propose a sampling-based estimation strategy within Owen's multilinear extension framework, combining stratified sampling with coalition leverage scores. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining explanation accuracy.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: Learning from Duality in Neural Network Field Theories
nodes.authors: Pietro Capuozzo, Brandon Robinson, Benjamin Suzzoni
nodes.summary: We develop neural realizations of positive-level Wess-Zumino-Witten models using bosonic Wakimoto and fermionic Fourier-Berezin fields. Level-rank duality connects the charged sectors of the fermionic construction, where explicit neural observables recover conformal block data and enable the transfer of information about unknown correlators between paired theories. We also show that distinct neural presentations of the same continuum current algebra exhibit different finite-width behavior, with approximation accuracy depending on architecture, regulator, and parameter distribution. These results connect the exact mathematical structure of conformal field theory with the expressive and computational properties of neural field theories.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: Differentiable Exact Learning
nodes.authors: Hristo Papazov, Francesco D'Angelo, Nicolas Flammarion
nodes.summary: We introduce a framework for differentiable exact learning that couples an unbounded external environment to a state-tracking neural controller, which we train on policy-trajectory observations (PTOs): expert behavior traces that expose observations and actions while hiding internal states. In addition to the learning framework, we introduce Differentiable Finite-State Transducers (DFSTs) which use multilinear updates, support log-parallel training, and emulate arbitrary finite-state controllers, yielding computational universality through environmental interaction. From tiny training datasets, compact DFSTs achieve extreme length generalization on arithmetic and universal-simulation tasks. We replicate the success of DFSTs on RNNs and GRUs, thereby supporting a broader learning recipe: State-Tracking Controller + Unbounded External Environment + PTOs = Extreme Length Generalization. Beyond length generalization, our metric-extraction protocol recovers interpretable discrete controllers from trained DFSTs, which we prove equivalent to the target arithmetic and universal-simulation algorithms. Furthermore, for our Softmax DFST models, simply taking $\mathrm{argmax}$ over the transition probabilities yields discrete controllers which provably exactly perform universal Turing-machine simulation and binary arithmetic. Proving exact learning for the neural controllers requires assumptions, which we empirically support. We make our code, training recipes, model weights, and proof checkers publicly available at https://github.com/fanagor/DEL.

nodes.title: RESILAGENT: A Three-Pillar Architecture for Cyber-Physical Resilience in Electrical Power and Energy Systems
nodes.authors: Nikolaos Kekatos, Georgios Koutidis, Konstantinos Antonakopoulos, Stylianos Basagiannis, Sokratis Katsikas, Georgios Kavallieratos, Alexios Lekidis, Tom Nianios, Elpiniki Papageorgiou
nodes.summary: Electrical Power and Energy Systems face hybrid threats that combine cyber intrusions, physical sabotage and climate-driven stress, and routinely outpace today's siloed monitoring stacks. We present RESILAGENT, a concept architecture organised around three operational pillars, Sensing & Data Intelligence, Resilience Analytics & Reporting, and Incident Response & Recovery, mediated by a Cloud-based Orchestrator and exercised through a closed Detect-Simulate-Decide-Sign loop. The framework fuses agentic artificial intelligence and multimodal large language models for cross-modal detection, real-time digital twins for what-if simulation, and a permissioned blockchain anchor for tamper-evident threat intelligence and CER/NIS2-aligned evidence. We instantiate it on two scenarios, a transmission operator under coordinated cyber compromise, sabotage and heatwave, and a distribution operator under a supply-chain compromise during a storm, and report an IEEE-bus micro-benchmark that quantifies each pillar through false-data-injection attack detection, cyber-physical fusion lift, N-1 contingency screening and anchor cost.

nodes.title: Generative AI and the Crisis of Higher Education Assessments: Examining 'AI-Proofing' Strategies for College-Level Assessments
nodes.authors: Bonam Mingole, Davis Yadav, Hui Min Lee, S. Shyam Sundar, Amulya Yadav
nodes.summary: Higher education is confronting an academic-integrity challenge unlike any in its history. Students can now outsource homework, take-home assignments, and online examinations to large language models (LLMs) that complete them in seconds. Existing research on evaluating LLM performance on academic assessments has focused largely on standardized examinations, or on questions from college-level courses drawn from a single discipline. Far less is known about how LLMs perform on college-level assessment questions spanning multiple disciplines, that instructors have purposely designed to be AI-resistant, and about which features of such questions, if any, meaningfully constrain LLM performance. We address this gap by collecting 75 questions from authentic college coursework assessments, spanning 17 disciplines, which were contributed by 37 faculty members from ten U.S. universities and one U.K. university. Of these, 61 questions were intentionally designed by faculty members to be 'LLM-proof', while the remaining 14 questions were sourced from online courses. We then (i) evaluate three state-of-the-art LLMs' ability to correctly answer these questions with and without supplementary course materials; (ii) identify five strategies, through thematic analysis, that faculty used to make their questions harder for LLMs to solve; and (iii) test whether these strategies impact LLMs' ability to answer the questions accurately. Our experimental results show that the best-performing model scored approximately 83% without supplementary course materials and 85% with them, and we observed noteworthy differences across models, answer formats, and instructor tweaking strategies. We discuss implications for assessment design, academic-integrity policy, and the broader ethics of deploying LLMs in educational settings.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: Generative Data Augmentation Without External Data: An Empirical and Theoretical Study on Deep Networks
nodes.authors: Daniel Kua, Yan Song
nodes.summary: Generative data augmentation adds samples from generative models to a classifier's training set. Many influential studies use generators pre-trained on large external datasets, and so mix the value of synthetic data with knowledge transferred through pretraining. We study the case without external data, where each generator learns only from the classifier's own training set, and ask when and why adding generated samples to that training set raises or lowers the classifier's test accuracy. We train classifiers with four backbones on six datasets, two of them medical, adding samples from four generators. We bound the excess risk of a classifier trained with synthetic data, that is, how far its population risk can lie above the minimum risk within its hypothesis class. The bound charges synthetic data for the total variation distance between the real and generated distributions and credits synthetic data for a larger training set. The gain from adding synthetic data, the fall in population risk, is at most the excess risk of the real-only classifier, which trains on the real images alone. Read through the bound, the experiments suggest that synthetic data help most when our classifiers detect only a small discrepancy between the generated and real data and the real-only classifier has room to improve, and that synthetic data help little or hurt when the detected discrepancy is large. Generators with a larger lower bound on the total variation distance, a bound that we estimate from our own classifiers, tend to help less on five of the six datasets, and on the CIFAR datasets the most accurate backbone gains the least. The bound gives these directions but not the size of the largest gains, most of which traditional augmentation also reaches at the same number of optimizer steps.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: Warm Starting Neural Dynamics Models From Few Jacobian Samples
nodes.authors: Maxime Rochkoulets, Joppe De Jonghe, Mariya Ishteva
nodes.summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) leverages a model of the environment, used for planning and generating samples without interacting with the real world. Motivated by evidence that informed initialization significantly improves the efficiency of MBRL, we propose TDec-Init, an algorithm to warm-start neural dynamics models using transition Jacobians. Using a decoupling algorithm based on the decomposition of a tensor of stacked Jacobian samples, we recover weights and flexible nonlinearities, and use them to initialize a feedforward neural network. In the low-data regime, we show on several benchmark environments that our approach outperforms random initialization and value training, and either matches or outperforms Sobolev training, while requiring fewer training steps between episodes.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: A Scalable Multi Task Learning Framework for Modeling Demographic Disagreements in Annotation Tasks
nodes.authors: Soumyajit Gupta, Maria De-Arteaga, Matthew Lease
nodes.summary: Annotators from different demographic backgrounds often disagree in systematic ways due to varying lived experiences, cultural contexts, and their relationship to the content. When such disagreement occurs, one group's perspective may sometimes warrant prioritization because they hold an epistemically advantaged standpoint or bear greater stake in the outcome. For example, when assessing toxicity of posts on social media, it may be important to prioritize a targeted group's viewpoint. We propose a Stakeholder-Aware Joint Multi-Task Learning (SAJ-MTL) framework to jointly model demographic disagreement both across- and within- annotator groups. The model uses conditional gradient routing to handle sparsity induced by group-conditional labeling, and parameterization supports customized weighting of groups in different task settings. SAJ-MTL improves group-level performance in toxicity detection through better context-aware understanding of demographic-sensitive content. Only annotator group-membership information is required, which is more practical than existing methods requiring more privacy-invasive individual-level annotator details. Our scalable architecture is also computationally efficient to support large-scale deployment.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: Out of Sight, Into Memory: Compact Visual Latents Retain Local Evidence in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing
nodes.authors: Meng Tang, Siyuan Du, Yuxin Liu, Shuaishuai Cao, Di Wang, Haonan Guo
nodes.summary: Question answering over ultra-high-resolution (UHR) remote sensing scenes poses a tension for multimodal large language models: global overviews obscure small objects and local attributes, whereas detailed crops consume substantial context. Compressing inspected crops into short sequences of continuous visual latents offers a compact memory once crop tokens are discarded, yet diagnostic studies on natural images find that models often ignore latent content, leaving unclear whether compact latents can retain fine-grained targets lost in downsampled UHR remote sensing scenes. To isolate evidence retention from region selection, we encode high-resolution crops into latent memory tokens for frozen backbones and evaluate both their predictive utility and content dependence. Across two generations of Qwen-VL on LRS-GRO, a 64-token memory achieves 7.6- to 9.9-fold compression of retained crop tokens and improves accuracy by 2.5 to 4.8 percentage points over the downsampled global image alone, recovering most of the high-resolution crop gain with consistent behavior on XLRS-Bench. Substituting memory from another image or another region of the same scene reduces accuracy by 5.8 to 7.4 percentage points and yields lower accuracy than removing memory altogether, demonstrating that predictions depend on the encoded regional evidence. Restoring the source crop within the same model reduces the accuracy loss caused by zeroing or removing memory. These findings establish that compact visual latents retain useful local evidence in UHR remote sensing and identify evidence availability as a key factor governing their contribution.

nodes.title: FaceJev: Direct Visual Decisions for Face Forgery Detection
nodes.authors: Siran Peng, Tianshuo Zhang, Yibo Xue, Ajian Liu, Haoyuan Zhang, Weisong Zhao, Shuhuan Chen, Xiangyu Zhu, Zhen Lei
nodes.summary: Face forgery detection methods often perform well on seen manipulations but generalize poorly to unseen ones. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) can recognize facial parts and assess their visual plausibility. Existing MLLM-based methods typically express these judgments through textual explanations, but seldom treat individual part decisions as explicit learning targets. We present FaceJev, an MLLM-based method for face forgery detection through direct visual decisions. Following the Jev formulation, FaceJev answers eight independent questions about facial parts using a shared image encoding and reads anomaly probabilities from the native answer logits. A face is classified as forged if any part is predicted to be abnormal, directly linking the detection result to the part decisions. We construct PartForensics, a dataset of approximately 160k images with binary anomaly targets for the eight facial parts, to supervise these decisions. We further propose FS-GRPO, which optimizes each part decision through an exact reward comparison with its alternative, using both detection and part rewards. FaceJev outperforms the strongest baseline by 7.25 percentage points on unseen manipulations. Extensive ablation studies validate our design choices and the effectiveness of the main components.
nodes.subject: Spatial AI

nodes.title: ScenarioForge: Resource-Grounded Generation and Execution Validation of Cyber Exercises
nodes.authors: Jaime C. Acosta, Anantaa Kotal, Aritran Piplai
nodes.summary: Cyber-range and capture-the-flag scenario construction remains labor-intensive because authors must coordinate infrastructure, vulnerable services, attack paths, artifacts, and success conditions. LLMs can propose detailed exercises, but plausible descriptions do not guarantee deployable software or verifiable objectives. We present ScenarioForge, which turns high-level requirements into resource-grounded topologies, services, traffic, segmentation, and challenge chains, then instantiates and validates them in the Common Open Research Emulator (CORE). The ScenarioForge Execution Dataset contains 226 materialized scenarios covering 294 Vulhub images and all 85 custom-built challenge-resource generators developed with our AI-assisted scaffolding. All 226 passed construction, preview, sequencing, deployment, strict runtime validation, and live artifact checks; their 867 steps, each an individually verifiable challenge objective, comprise 457 vulnerability-backed and 410 generated-resource-backed instances. In a separate 50-prompt matched benchmark, ScenarioForge+Qwen3.8 and ScenarioForge+GPT5.6 each achieved 50/50 (100%) topology/build success and 160/160 intent fields; direct frontier generation reached 41/50 builds and 147/160 fields only with the full cumulative scaffold: structure, vocabulary, policy, and container-image guidance. The test still omitted ScenarioForge's downstream challenge-resource generation, dependency/flag sequencing, deployment, and live validation. The artifacts support operationally rich, reproducible exercises for training and evaluation.
