nodes.title: Beyond Recall Saturation: Scaling Hard-Negative Reranker Training for Industrial Legal Retrieval
nodes.authors: Yunhan Li, Mingjie Xie, Zeyang Shi, Gengshen Wu, Min Yang
nodes.summary: Industrial retrieval systems often improve quality by enlarging embedding candidate pools or adopting complex training pipelines. We show that, under a sufficiently large but practical candidate pool, embedding recall exhibits diminishing returns, motivating a closer examination of reranker quality. On Chinese legal retrieval benchmarks, embedding top-300 reaches a high-recall operating region, while relevant evidence may still be ranked below the output cutoff. We compare hard-negative strategies for reranker training, including embedding-mined, self-mined, and dynamic-negative variants, under aligned retrieval protocols that evaluate reranking after candidate retrieval. Among the evaluated staged configurations, an embedding-to-self-mined pipeline provides a favorable trade-off; additional dynamic stages do not improve all held-out metrics. The selected pipeline scales from a 0.6B to a 4B reranker. Relative to the native 4B reranker, the trained 4B Stage2 model improves reported metrics on the STARD and CSAID benchmarks and on an internal development set, and is preferred in 72.4\% of non-tied comparisons on 410 de-identified, reconstructed internal operational-query inputs in a latency-sensitive offline preference evaluation. These results support evaluating the retrieval and reranking stages separately when selecting an optimization target for industrial retrieval systems.
nodes.subject: Computation and Language

nodes.title: Pluralistic Alignment in Large Language Models: Objectives, Human References, and Preference Representations
nodes.authors: Meng-Chen Wu, Umesh Bodhwani
nodes.summary: Pluralistic alignment aims to represent meaningful variation in human preferences rather than collapse heterogeneous judgments into a single target. Yet existing work often mixes three distinct questions: what pluralistic behavior a model should exhibit, whose preferences define the reference, and what evidence is sufficient to demonstrate success. We organize the literature around a two-layer taxonomy. Layer 1 distinguishes representing a range of human-supported viewpoints (Overton Pluralism), adapting faithfully to a specified perspective or preference condition (Steerable Pluralism), and matching the response distribution observed in a target population (Distributional Pluralism). Layer 2 distinguishes aggregate populations, countries and regions, and subgroups as human references. Preference representation, implementation mechanism, modality, and evidence quality are treated as cross-cutting design choices rather than additional forms of pluralism. We synthesize a protocol-bounded corpus of 70 works on pluralistic alignment and neighboring areas, using the objective-by-human-reference matrix to map existing approaches and identify underexplored combinations. The coded literature concentrates on Steerable Pluralism and Distributional Pluralism, while eligible Overton Pluralism work appears only at the aggregate-population level under our stated protocol. We then connect each objective to the evidence needed to support it, including perspective validity, conditional fidelity, distributional fidelity, support preservation, and uncertainty in subgroup estimates. Together, the taxonomy and evaluation framework clarify what current methods establish, where their claims exceed their evidence, and how future systems can represent disagreement without mistaking variation for faithful representation.
nodes.subject: Computation and Language

nodes.title: Beyond Geometric Closure: Measuring and Diagnosing Mechanical Consistency in Visual Dynamics
nodes.authors: Qibin Gu, Yunfeng Yan
nodes.summary: Visual accuracy, geometric validity, and agreement with applied forces are distinct requirements for visual dynamics. We introduce a diagnostic framework that connects reaction-free SI measurements to controlled interventions on coordinate readout, training integration, and actuator response. Reference replay calibrates the measurement path, while continuous scoring exposes progress against fixed engineering targets. With three seeds per setting, we evaluate KeyCLD and CON across 343 planar assemblies at 64/256 pixels and V-JEPA + AC and LingBot-VA on 100 shared spatial test assemblies. CON reduces image MSE by 37.6%/37.2% relative to persistence, yet neither planar model attains valid native geometry. At 256 pixels, calibrated RGB replay places forecast errors far above the reference measurement floor. Exact-state KeyCLD has identical geometric pass rates under Euler and RK4 training, yet its score rises from 52.65 to 64.30 as force and energy errors decrease. In both spatial pathways, CAD/IK reconstruction restores geometry while mean actuator residuals exceed five times the engineering targets. These diagnoses distinguish coordinate correction, numerical improvement, and persistent force-response errors, guiding targeted improvements to visual dynamics.
nodes.subject: 3D Vision

nodes.title: Goal Images Are Control Targets: Spatially-Grounded Goal-Image Synthesis for Robotic Manipulation
nodes.authors: Riddhi Chatterjee, Ritish Shrirao, Kushagra Mehrotra, Viswanath Gopalakrishnan
nodes.summary: Goal-conditioned manipulation policies are steered by a goal image, a picture of the desired post-manipulation scene synthesized from the current observation and a language instruction. The prevailing assumption is that better image-editing quality yields better goals, so goal generators are built and compared using general image-editing metrics. We show this assumption is false. Across two independent goal-conditioned policies on CALVIN, the image editors that top aggregate editing-quality leaderboards (Gemini 3 Pro Image and GPT Image 1.5) produce worse control targets than our proposed far smaller finetuned open models, and the gap widens sharply for the multi-step (long-horizon) tasks robots actually face. A per-dimension analysis explains why. Downstream policy success is governed almost entirely by manipulation adherence (selecting the right object and the right final state; Spearman $ρ\approx 0.9$ with success), while photorealism and aesthetic fidelity, precisely where large proprietary editors excel, are uncorrelated with success ($ρ\approx 0$). This dissociation holds on both CALVIN and the real-world-aligned SIMPLER-Bridge benchmark. We then present SGE-Goal, a spatially-grounded decomposed editing framework that predicts initial and final 2D edit-region masks before goal-image synthesis. SGE-Goal turns open base models (FLUX.1 Kontext, FLUX.2 klein) into the strongest goal generators we evaluate on CALVIN, and second only to Gemini 3 Pro Image on SIMPLER-Bridge. Base models fine-tuned with SGE-Goal also hold up under chaining far better than the best proprietary editor, sustaining roughly seven times the success rate at the longest (five-step) chains. We release code, datasets, checkpoints, and a human-aligned diagnostic evaluator. Our results argue that goal generators must be selected by downstream utility, not by editing-quality leaderboards.
nodes.subject: Digital Human

nodes.title: ContactBench 1.0: A Benchmark for Everyday Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation
nodes.authors: Jingyi Xiang, Yixuan Wang, Jeannette Bohg, Wenzhen Yuan
nodes.summary: Contact-rich manipulation underlies many everyday human activities, yet evaluating robots on such tasks remains difficult: the tasks involve diverse contact behaviors and are hard to reproduce across laboratories. Drawing on observations of everyday human manipulation, we identify eight essential skills that provide a practical framework for studying contact-rich manipulation. We introduce ContactBench 1.0, an extensible benchmark that instantiates these skills through 36 reference tasks and more than 40 object assets. The assets capture task-relevant geometry and contact behavior, can be fabricated reproducibly on consumer-grade 3D printers, and are each paired with a matching simulation model. Controlled task variations in both the real world and simulation enable evaluation of how well robot systems generalize. We evaluate recent representative vision-only and visual-tactile policy learning methods on six benchmark tasks. The results reveal that while vision-only policies struggle to perceive or react to contact events, visual-tactile policies do not meaningfully improve their performance, highlighting that contact-rich manipulation remains a significant challenge for current policy learning methods. By providing common task definitions alongside physical and simulated assets, ContactBench 1.0 offers a shared testbed for developing, evaluating, and comparing contact-rich manipulation systems. The benchmark will be open-sourced at https://jingyi-xiang.github.io/contactbench.

nodes.summary: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. The model accepts text and image inputs and produces text outputs, was trained on data from over a hundred languages, and is quantized to approximately 4-bit precision for efficient single-GPU inference. Muse Glimmer achieves state-of-the-art performance for its size class on agentic benchmarks, setting a new standard compared to the models of its size: Gemma4-31B and Qwen3.6-27B on tool use, multi-step planning, and agentic task completion. We release the model under the Apache 2.0 license to foster open-source development of capable, safe, local AI agents.

nodes.title: BanglaBBQ: A Bias Benchmark for Question Answering in the Bangladeshi Context
nodes.authors: Sumit Anthony Gomes, Yasin Rahman, Taeeba Tasnia, Faiza Nooren Suhita
nodes.summary: This paper presents BanglaBBQ, a question-answering bias benchmark designed to capture stereotypes grounded in the Bangladeshi context, in both Bangla and English. Following KoBBQ and PakBBQ, BanglaBBQ adapts the original Bias Benchmark for Question Answering (BBQ) by classifying its templates into three groups: directly translated (DT), modified to align target groups or contexts with Bangladesh (TM), and removed when deemed unsuitable for the Bangladeshi context (SR). This process retains 140 templates across six categories, comprising 76 DT and 64 TM templates. Five newly authored (NA) categories, based on stereotypes common in Bangladeshi society, are then added: marital status, age and political perception, regional origin, educational background, and mental-health status. Native Bangladeshi annotators judged all 466 newly authored templates, and 372 were retained because a strict majority of English annotators identified the intended target and rated the attitude as common enough. Each newly authored template is linked to a documented source and a verbatim quote from it. Each evaluated template also has a counter-stereotypical version of its disambiguated context. The dataset was evaluated using two open-weight models (Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B) and two closed models (GPT-4.1-mini and Gemini 2.5 Flash). All four lean towards the stereotyped person when the context is ambiguous, in both languages, and the effect of language differs by model, so English results do not predict behaviour in Bangla. On the adapted BBQ templates, both Qwen3 models are also less accurate when the context contradicts a stereotype than when it confirms it. On the newly authored templates, the closed models follow counter-stereotypical evidence almost perfectly, and all four models are more biased on the templates that annotators validated than on those they rejected.
nodes.subject: Computation and Language

nodes.title: Hippo: Training-Free Agent Self-Evolution via Hippocampal Replay
nodes.authors: Yutong Song, Jiang Wu, Yuxuan Ren, Tony Qin, Baoyuan Wang
nodes.summary: Motivated by recursive self-improvement (RSI), we study how LLM agents can learn through external memory without updating model parameters. Extracting useful experience from a single attempt is difficult: flawed reasoning can produce success, while poor execution can obscure a sound strategy. Preserving its value over time is also difficult: our accumulation baseline without consolidation initially improves but eventually performs below a no-memory baseline. Our key idea is to compare attempts at the same task to identify reusable decisions and refine when they apply. We introduce Hippo, a memory framework inspired by selective hippocampal encoding and replay that learns from these comparisons when shortcomings are diagnosed. It compares the resulting experience with existing memory to merge overlaps and resolve conflicts through explicit applicability conditions. This allows prior guidance to be revised without storing every lesson as a separate entry. Experiments on SWE-bench Verified, WebArena, and Mind2Web show performance gains in all three settings and substantially fewer retained experiences than the accumulation baseline. The gains extend across the evaluated base models of varying capabilities, indicating that memory-based adaptation remains useful even for highly capable models.
nodes.subject: Foundation Models

nodes.title: Measuring Data Diversity with Embeddings: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Diversity Measures
nodes.authors: Cantao Su, Anna Wegmann, Esther Ploeger, Dong Nguyen
nodes.summary: Diversity is a critical property of text corpora, with direct implications for training data curation, test set design, and model generalization. However, its measurement remains fragmented and poorly understood. Existing embedding-based diversity measures vary widely in how they are computed and can yield substantially different diversity scores on the same data, yet no systematic comparison of their empirical behaviour exists. We make two contributions toward addressing this gap. First, we present a taxonomy of 21 embedding-based diversity measures, organizing them into four families based on their underlying computations. Second, we introduce EmbDivBench, a benchmark that evaluates these measures along three conceptually distinct components (variety, balance and disparity) on both simulated and natural text data. Although Mean Pairwise Distance is the most commonly used measure, our experiments show that it is outperformed by several alternatives on the three diversity components, with Graph Entropy being the best choice overall. Lastly, we distil these findings into practical recommendations for diversity measure selection.

nodes.title: Table Serialization Determines Which Relations Language Models Preserve
nodes.authors: Junwei Ma, Arun Kumar Chithanar, Palash Goyal, Chul Lee
nodes.summary: We study how text serialization affects table lookup in instruction-tuned language models. Our diagnostic asks the model to find the row containing a specified value under one named column, then return the value under another named column in that same row. We render the same synthetic 256-cell tables in row-major form and in column-major form with each header placed beside its values, while varying the table aspect ratio across five shapes. Across three models, the better format changes with table shape: row-major performs better on tall tables, whereas column-major performs better on wide tables. At 64 x 4, row-major leads by 42.3-54.0 percentage points; at 4 x 64, column-major leads by 35.0-59.0 points. Mapping wrong answers back to their source cells reveals a complementary error pattern: row-major tends to preserve the correct row but lose the target column, while column-major tends to preserve the correct column but lose the row. We use the term relational locality to describe this pattern: serialization keeps one relation locally available while making the other depend on positional alignment. A separate non-tabular ordering experiment supports this interpretation. Thus, apparent width-related failures in text-serialized tables depend on linearization, not table shape alone.
nodes.subject: Computation and Language

nodes.title: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning with General Utilities via Neural Dual Critics
nodes.authors: Ankur Naskar, Vaneet Aggarwal
nodes.summary: Reinforcement learning with general utilities optimizes nonlinear functionals of policy-induced occupancy measures. We develop a natural actor-critic method for concave RLGU objectives using an exact variational dual representation, whose existence follows from concavity and differentiability, with explicit constructions for a broad class of separable occupancy utilities. Rather than estimating the occupancy measure and then forming the policy-gradient pseudo-reward, our method learns this pseudo-reward directly as a function of the state-action pair using a neural critic. The critic is trained by projected stochastic updates, while multilevel Monte Carlo combines outputs across training horizons to control its bias at logarithmic expected cost. Our analysis separates conditional actor bias from estimator second moments and accounts explicitly for dual optimization, critic approximation, and neural linearization errors. Under policy-transfer, dual-stability, and local critic-regularity conditions, the method achieves $\widetilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$ global convergence above policy, critic-class, and finite-width approximation errors using $\widetilde{O}(T)$ expected environment transitions and reference samples. For a fixed critic representation, this yields $\widetilde{O}(ε^{-2})$ sampling complexity above the approximation floor, covering infinite state-action spaces and occupancy utilities beyond fixed finite vectors of returns.
nodes.subject: Machine Learning

nodes.title: Transport What Shares the Conduction Pathway: Normal-Anchored SPD Geometric Transport for Source-Free Patient Adaptation of Holter and Patch ECG
nodes.authors: JinKook Kim
nodes.summary: Continuous electrocardiogram (ECG) streams are dominated by normal beats (87.9-98.6% of the label-free adaptation prefix in our four databases), and patient-specific waveform distortion is not shared by every beat class; under this combination, source-free and test-time adaptation methods that assume class-balanced target batches collapse. We propose Normal-Anchored Geometric Transport (NAGT, GA_NS), which estimates a closed-form symmetric positive-definite congruence map from label-free normal anchors in the first 5 min of each recording and applies it only to the normal and supraventricular prototypes, keeping the ventricular and fusion prototypes fixed. Decision rules were set on MIT-BIH and the rate-invariant RR head was adopted after the development databases (INCART, SVDB) had been opened; the frozen model was then evaluated once under a pre-specified locked evaluation protocol on the held-out Icentia11k chest-patch cohort. In 493 patients (973 recordings, 3,615,388 evaluated beats), NAGT raised the arrhythmia macro-F1 J from 34.5% to 48.7% ($ΔJ$ = +14.1 [+8.6, +19.3] pp; non-AF 43.9% to 59.8%) and outperformed all five Holm-adjusted comparators, including AdaBN, Tent and T3A. In post hoc analyses of the frozen outputs, ventricular false alarms fell by 68% (41.1 to 13.2 per hour) and 98.3% of normal beats stayed outside the alarm classes. Adaptation takes 5.8 ms per record without back-propagation.
nodes.subject: Machine Learning

nodes.title: When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
nodes.authors: Yichuan Chen, Xin Wang
nodes.summary: Language models sometimes repeat verbatim until the generation limit. We study the exit rather than the entrance: given that a span has already been repeated $n$ times, when is escape still possible? Along the loop the context is deterministic, so the probability that a loop survives $m$ more repetitions is, under any sampler, a product of per-step continuation probabilities computable from one forward pass. A lock, where this probability stays exactly one, is its limiting case. Pure sampling never locks; top-$p$ with threshold $π>1/2$ locks a position exactly when the continuation probability reaches $π$. A bounded penalty can leave a position locked; a penalty that outgrows the model's preference for the loop over unseen tokens guarantees escape under top-$p$. The same analysis shows a blind spot in the widely deployed DRY sampler: its sequence breakers cap the penalty at $λb^{g-1-a}$ for loops whose longest breaker-free run has $g$ tokens. On eleven open models, 61% of locked units with $g=6$ stay locked under DRY and 0.2% with $g=8$. In free generation with llama.cpp, all 199 loops that survive DRY, on six models, have $g\le 7$. We propose a count term that grows exponentially with the number of verbatim recurrences, up to its look-back window, and closes this blind spot. Added to DRY (DRY-C), it cuts loops in 1,800 structured generations on five models from 167 to 34, and loops reaching the length limit from 150 to 0, with reasoning accuracy and item coverage on par with DRY. DRY's own length term costs 2.5 to 14.2 points of accuracy on GSM8K and MATH-500; used in its place, the count term keeps the default sampler's accuracy and leaves one of the 1,800 generations at the limit.
nodes.subject: Generative Search Engines

nodes.title: O-SCD++: Replay-Free Online Scene Change Detection via Recursive Evidence Fusion
nodes.authors: Chamuditha Jayanga Galappaththige, Jason Lai, Lloyd Windrim, Timothy Patten, Donald G. Dansereau, Niko Suenderhauf, Dimity Miller
nodes.summary: Online scene change detection requires an autonomous agent to detect what has changed in a previously mapped environment while it is still on site, observing from unconstrained viewpoints and without access to future observations. This causal setting is strictly harder than offline detection, and online methods have long trailed offline accuracy. Our earlier method, O-SCD, closed that gap at over 10 frames per second, but its multi-view fusion is an iterative optimization that refits a change field over a 3D Gaussian splatting map of the reference scene to all past observations at every frame. This step consumes over half of the per-frame budget and forces accuracy to be traded against speed. We present O-SCD++, a replay-free formulation that eliminates this trade-off. Because the reference map stays fixed, rendering the change field is a linear operation. Each new observation can therefore be carried onto the map's Gaussians by a single backward pass of the renderer and fused by a two-scalar recursion per Gaussian. Past observations are never stored or revisited. O-SCD++ also makes the change/no-change decision without labels or iterative optimization. It sets each frame's threshold to the exact minimizer of O-SCD's self-supervised objective over threshold masks, using one sort, and the distance to this threshold gives a per-pixel decision margin that predicts errors. On PASLCD, O-SCD++ improves change detection accuracy (mIoU) from $0.489$ to $0.575$ and throughput from $11.8$ to $25.6$ frames per second, exceeding O-SCD's offline result while remaining causal.
nodes.subject: 3D Vision

nodes.title: Pluralistic Alignment in Large Language Models: Objectives, Human References, and Preference Representations
nodes.authors: Meng-Chen Wu, Umesh Bodhwani
nodes.summary: Pluralistic alignment aims to represent meaningful variation in human preferences rather than collapse heterogeneous judgments into a single target. Yet existing work often mixes three distinct questions: what pluralistic behavior a model should exhibit, whose preferences define the reference, and what evidence is sufficient to demonstrate success. We organize the literature around a two-layer taxonomy. Layer 1 distinguishes representing a range of human-supported viewpoints (Overton Pluralism), adapting faithfully to a specified perspective or preference condition (Steerable Pluralism), and matching the response distribution observed in a target population (Distributional Pluralism). Layer 2 distinguishes aggregate populations, countries and regions, and subgroups as human references. Preference representation, implementation mechanism, modality, and evidence quality are treated as cross-cutting design choices rather than additional forms of pluralism. We synthesize a protocol-bounded corpus of 70 works on pluralistic alignment and neighboring areas, using the objective-by-human-reference matrix to map existing approaches and identify underexplored combinations. The coded literature concentrates on Steerable Pluralism and Distributional Pluralism, while eligible Overton Pluralism work appears only at the aggregate-population level under our stated protocol. We then connect each objective to the evidence needed to support it, including perspective validity, conditional fidelity, distributional fidelity, support preservation, and uncertainty in subgroup estimates. Together, the taxonomy and evaluation framework clarify what current methods establish, where their claims exceed their evidence, and how future systems can represent disagreement without mistaking variation for faithful representation.
nodes.subject: Computation and Language

nodes.title: FlashRT-PAI: Fast Kernels Are Not Fast Pipelines for Physical AI
nodes.authors: Liang Su, David Chen, Jason Li, Kevin Guo, Teresa Lv
nodes.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA), video-action (VA), and world action models (WAMs) form the backbone of modern physical AI systems, yet their real-time single-batch inference remains a defining bottleneck. Latency is dominated not by individual kernel computation, but by system-level overhead: thousands of short kernel launches, intermediate data movement across operator boundaries, and redundant recomputation across consecutive decisions. General-purpose graph compilers cannot address these costs, as they optimize individual calls in isolation and lack visibility into cross-call state semantics and global pipeline structure. We present FLASHRT-PAI, a low-latency inference engine built around model-hardware pipeline co-design rather than isolated kernel optimization. FLASHRT-PAI combines three core mechanisms: deep kernel fusion with launch overlap eliminates inter-operator boundaries and launch gaps; an execution contract formalizes the pipeline's stage DAG, update rates, and named buffers to enable cross-decision state reuse and selective refresh; and execution-state capsules enable fast snapshot, restore, and fork of persistent pipeline state. The system also supports drop-in acceleration of unmodified PyTorch models via parity- and latency-gated kernel replacement. Evaluation covers six policies on RTX 5090 and four on Jetson AGX Thor. At matched 16-bit precision, FLASHRT-PAI is 1.3-3.7x faster than official compiled paths. Combining pipeline co-design with reduced precision delivers 3.38-12.66x speedup over official eager implementations. In LIBERO-10, four-bit pi0.5 achieves 94.04% success on Thor and 93.32% on RTX 5090, compared with 92.4% for the measured official FP16 reference. FLASHRT-PAI is open source, distributed via Hugging Face Kernel Hub, and its opt-in pi0.5 kernels have been adopted into the LeRobot framework.
nodes.subject: Video World Models

nodes.title: UniField++: A Unified Agentic Framework with Loop Reasoning for MRI Field-Strength Enhancement
nodes.authors: Yiyang Lin, Chenhui Wang, Tianliang Yao, Pengli Zhu, Shuaibo Li, Zijun Sun, Yiming Deng, Yixuan Yuan
nodes.summary: MRI field-strength enhancement seeks to combine the accessibility of low-field scanners with the image quality of high-field scanners. Yet, existing methods remain prone to anatomical hallucinations, as uniform processing leaves difficult brain regions insufficiently examined and scarce paired data limit their learning of how tissue contrast and anatomical visibility change across field strengths. To address these challenges, we propose UniField++, a two-agent framework that unifies enhancement tasks across multiple field-strength transitions, including 64mT-to-3T and 3T-to-7T. Unified learning allows both the VLM-based planner and the flow-matching-based enhancer to draw on field-dependent image characteristics observed across tasks, rather than relying on a single transition. Trained with radiologists' annotations of hallucination-prone regions and corresponding correction plans, the planner predicts regional risk and formulates targeted restoration strategies. Guided by these plans, the enhancer performs loop reasoning along the flow-matching trajectory, repeatedly processing high-risk regions for additional refinement. Together, cross-transition learning and risk-guided refinement support anatomically faithful enhancement across field strengths. Across the evaluated tasks, UniField++ improves PSNR by an average of 2.74 dB and SSIM by 14.05 percentage points over comparison methods, with corresponding gains of 3.97 dB and 13.92 percentage points over the ablation baseline. It also maintains enhancement quality on an external cohort with an unseen field strength and improves downstream whole-brain segmentation Macro Dice by an average of 0.1457 over the original low-field images. Code is available at https://github.com/CUHK-AIM-Group/UniField_plusplus.
nodes.subject: End-to-End AD

nodes.title: TorchTPU - A Hybrid Eager/Compiled Architecture for Native PyTorch Execution on TPU
nodes.authors: Claudio Basile, Michael Voznesensky, Gunhyun Park, Ben Wilson, Parker Holloway, Zhanyong Wan, Vlad Belous, Manish Khanna, Paul Ganssle, Kevin Gleason, Andrew Dame, Brendan Folie, Bhavya Bahl, Haifeng Jin, Pedro Goncalves Mokarzel, Arian Arfaian, Luke Boyer, Chi Zhang, Yiling Yuan, Adam Mainz, Aditya Patel, Huangze Tang, Jay Gan, Lizzie Liang, Will Froom, Tushar Agarwal, Karlo Basioli, Theotime Combes, Emilio Cota, Minos Papadopoulos, Tudor Pipernea, Yarong Mu, Qi Zhou, Yaoshiang Ho, Aleksey Vlasenko, Alexander Brauckmann, Ziyin Huang, Jack Oh, Jerry Hsu, Tanvi Bajpai, Jialei Chen, Wenjun Gu, Chintan Shah, Chris Chan, Sayce Falk, Chris Jones, Rob Torres, Kat Ko, Lee Howes, Freya Azad, Andi Gavrilescu, Joe Pamer, Bill Jia
nodes.summary: TorchTPU is an open-source collaboration between Google and Meta that introduces a native and principled PyTorch backend for Google TPUs. It enables seamless out-of-the-box model execution and TPU migration while delivering industry-competitive inference and training performance through eager execution optimizations, torch.compile integration, and native hardware acceleration.

nodes.title: No Eyes, No Problem: What Does Touch Contribute to Blind Baoding Ball Manipulation?
nodes.authors: Ayush Deshmukh, Nalin Agarwal, Elle Miller, Sethu Vijayakumar
nodes.summary: Humans manipulate objects within their hands through touch alone with remarkable ease, but for robots, achieving sustained real-world manipulation without vision remains an open challenge. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can generate sophisticated blind manipulation policies in simulation, transferring them to a real dexterous hand remains hindered by continuously changing contacts, motion-induced tactile information drift, and the gap between simulated and physical dynamics. We study this problem through Baoding ball rotation on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, using only proprioception and binary tactile feedback as observations. We achieve successful zero-shot transfer through a combination of a sensor-aligned, coupling-aware embodiment in simulation, tactile calibration, and two novel episodic domain randomisations: slew-rate action limits and STuck-AT Taxels. On the physical hand, the policy achieves sustained blind Baoding rotation, completing $\textbf{225 consecutive $\mathbf{180^\circ}$ rotations (112.5 full rotations) at $\sim0.36 \;\text{rot/s}$}$ in a single continuous trial without any vision or object-state information. Furthermore, we evaluate the contribution of tactile sensing relative to proprioception alone and identify the hand regions where tactile information is most important. This is the strongest reported hardware result for Baoding ball manipulation in both rotation count and speed, irrespective of the sensing modality used. By effectively bridging the sim-to-real gap, our framework sets a new benchmark for sustained tactile-driven dexterous manipulation on physical hardware.
nodes.subject: Robotics

nodes.title: Robotic Spatiotemporal Editing: A Unified Interface for Controllable Action Generation via Masked Action Reconstruction
nodes.authors: Yanbang Li, Bu He, Yi Tian, Yu-Chiao Huang, Chenyu Zhang, Ruoqu Chen, Yuanzhe Liu, Yuxiang Gao, Mengdi Xu
nodes.summary: Generative policies can synthesize robot behaviors, yet controlling and editing them through diverse spatiotemporal references remains challenging. In the real world, human intent requires robot behaviors that satisfy constraints on where, when, and how actions are executed. Our key insight is that spatiotemporal control references, such as keypoints, flows, orientations, and keyposes, can be viewed as partial specifications of the same temporal Cartesian action space. We introduce the MAP (Masked Action Space) interface to unify these action references and formulate controllable manipulation as an action inpainting problem. Our Inpainting Policy (IP) reconstructs missing action dimensions of the end-effector, combining progress-guided alignment with multi-mask training supporting unseen action-constraint combinations. We further adopt a training-free RePaint variant that iteratively inpaints the action during denoising to reduce control error. On ManiSkill and LIBERO-10, our policy achieves average task success rates of 92.67% and 64.67%, respectively.Real-world experiments demonstrate spatiotemporal control with average positional and rotational errors of 44.3 mm and 7°, respectively, showing that our policy can use diverse references to guide executable robot behaviors.

nodes.title: Algorithm Modelization: Transforming Optimization Algorithms into Evolvable Intelligence
nodes.authors: Jian Yao, Zhiyao Zhang, Yichen Li, Xingyu Wu, Kay Chen Tan
nodes.summary: Can algorithms be learned and evolved as models, rather than repeatedly redesigned as programs? We explore this question by introducing Algorithm Modelization, a new paradigm that turns iterative algorithms into trainable models. Its central idea is to regard algorithm execution trajectories as computational experience: by learning how algorithmic states evolve over iterations, a model can internalize the knowledge embodied in existing algorithms, reproduce their computational behaviors, and further evolve beyond them through training. As a first realization of this paradigm, we modelize iterative optimization as an autoregressive process, where preceding generations constitute the computational context for generating the next population. We develop a dimension-independent population-temporal architecture to capture both population interactions and iterative dynamics, together with an imitation-to-surpassing learning framework that first acquires algorithmic knowledge from heterogeneous teachers and then improves the resulting optimizer directly through optimization feedback. The modelized optimizer consequently goes beyond reproducing individual algorithms: it consolidates heterogeneous search knowledge into a single trainable model, achieves stronger optimization capability through subsequent improvement, and generalizes its acquired knowledge across problems and substantially larger unseen dimensions. More fundamentally, Algorithm Modelization makes algorithmic capability accumulable through learning, where new algorithms and problem-solving experience can become training resources for progressively improving the model. Our results establish a promising path from manually designed algorithms toward general algorithm models that learn, generalize, and evolve from computational experience.
nodes.subject: Embodied Intelligence

nodes.title: CatchUp: Depth-Aware Re-Admission of Visual Tokens for Efficient Large Vision-Language Models
nodes.authors: Eunju Park, Uiwon Hwang
nodes.summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) repeatedly process hundreds of visual tokens across decoder layers, incurring substantial computation and memory costs. Existing visual-token reduction methods often irreversibly discard tokens despite depth-varying query relevance. Although recoverable routing allows excluded tokens to return, re-admitted tokens retain stale hidden states after bypassing intermediate decoder transformations. Thus, token recoverability does not guarantee representation readiness at the current decoder depth. Under a fixed routing trajectory at a 64-token budget, replacing stale re-admitted states with current-depth oracle representations improves average RefCOCO Acc@0.5 from 18.96 to 23.18, revealing the impact of representation staleness. We propose CatchUp, a training-free framework combining reversible visual-token routing with Local Transition Correction (LTC). CatchUp repeatedly re-evaluates query-conditioned relevance over the complete visual-token set, preserving deferred tokens for later re-admission. LTC approximates their skipped representation evolution by transferring reference-to-current hidden-state transitions from semantically and spatially related active anchors. This correction improves alignment with current-depth oracle representations without recomputing the skipped decoder layers. Across three referring-expression grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the best grounding performance across all eight splits and the highest average multimodal retention among evaluated efficient methods at 64-, 128-, and 192-token budgets. At a 64-token budget, CatchUp processes 88.9% fewer active visual tokens per post-routing decoder interval, retains 92.17% of dense-model multimodal performance, and reduces end-to-end latency by 8.0%. Code is available at https://github.com/pej0918/CatchUp

nodes.title: Chinese Decision: A Family of Language Models for Single-Pass Probabilistic Decision-Making
nodes.authors: Qiang Yan
nodes.summary: Many language-based applications need a probability distribution over a small set of decisions rather than an open-ended response. We present Chinese Decision, a family of Chinese-language decision models that adapts pretrained causal language models to this interface. Each question is compiled into a shared instruction-and-candidate prompt; a single forward pass reads the final-position logits of the candidate letters and normalizes them over the valid options, without autoregressive answer generation. The interface covers Boolean judgments, categorical choices, and ordinal scores. We report three completed members built on Qwen3.5 0.8B, 2B, and 4B backbones, each trained for one epoch on the same 13.048 million decisions and released with a validation-fitted temperature and a Q8_0 quantization. On the full 307,900-decision CJ-Bench, the 4B model reaches 85.97% overall accuracy, 75.69% general-domain accuracy, and 84.00% average accuracy across medicine, law, and finance with a single checkpoint, above every reported baseline in each domain, at 1.00% expected calibration error. Between the 2B and 4B members, which share data, objective, and minimum batch, parent-clustered paired bootstrap intervals show gains in all four domains, largest in the two low-resource domains (+8.5 and +7.1 points), whereas the 2B gain over 0.8B in law is not statistically resolved. Analyses of the stored predictions further show that a single global temperature lowers pooled calibration error while worsening some domains, that larger members rank their own errors better for selective prediction, and that merging and quantization each change 0.4-1.1% of top-1 predictions while leaving aggregate metrics nearly unchanged. All comparisons rest on single training runs and imported baselines.

nodes.title: AM-Bench: A Unified Taxonomy and Evaluation Suite for Agentic Misalignment
nodes.authors: Eric Zhang, Terry Jingchen Zhang, Chijioke Ugwuanyi, Jerick Shi, Bernhard Schölkopf, Zhijing Jin
nodes.summary: As LLM-based agents are deployed with increasing autonomy in real-world environments, a critical failure mode emerges: agentic misalignment, where agents choose harmful actions over failure. However, existing safety benchmarks primarily evaluate whether agents comply with explicitly harmful instructions, leaving the conditions that cause agents to choose harmful actions poorly understood. To address this limitation, we propose AM-Bench, a unified taxonomy and 35 scenario evaluation benchmark spanning seven industries for agentic misalignment grounded in the fraud triangle, a well-established criminological framework explaining goal-directed misconduct. We adapt this framework to agentic environments and construct our evaluation suite and detection systems along three dimensions: perceived threat, perceived opportunity, and reasoning. We operationalize each dimension into structured subcategories rooted in prior theory: five threat categories derived from the instrumental convergence thesis, seven opportunity categories drawn from the Emergent Strategic Reasoning Risks (ESRR) taxonomy, and a novel four-question binary reasoning framework synthesized from prior literature. Our evaluation of 10 frontier models reveals a 62-percentage-point gap in misalignment across scenarios, with Gemini 3 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro exhibiting the highest levels of agentic misalignment while Claude Sonnet 4.6 displays near-zero rates across all conditions. Our reasoning framework further reveals that models may exhibit harmful behaviours without explicit situational awareness or explanation, complicating both mitigation and detection. AM-Bench scenarios and code are available at https://github.com/AI4Collaboration/Agentic-Misalignment-Bench

nodes.title: No Eyes, No Problem: What Does Touch Contribute to Blind Baoding Ball Manipulation?
nodes.authors: Ayush Deshmukh, Nalin Agarwal, Elle Miller, Sethu Vijayakumar
nodes.summary: Humans manipulate objects within their hands through touch alone with remarkable ease, but for robots, achieving sustained real-world manipulation without vision remains an open challenge. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can generate sophisticated blind manipulation policies in simulation, transferring them to a real dexterous hand remains hindered by continuously changing contacts, motion-induced tactile information drift, and the gap between simulated and physical dynamics. We study this problem through Baoding ball rotation on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, using only proprioception and binary tactile feedback as observations. We achieve successful zero-shot transfer through a combination of a sensor-aligned, coupling-aware embodiment in simulation, tactile calibration, and two novel episodic domain randomisations: slew-rate action limits and STuck-AT Taxels. On the physical hand, the policy achieves sustained blind Baoding rotation, completing $\textbf{225 consecutive $\mathbf{180^\circ}$ rotations (112.5 full rotations) at $\sim0.36 \;\text{rot/s}$}$ in a single continuous trial without any vision or object-state information. Furthermore, we evaluate the contribution of tactile sensing relative to proprioception alone and identify the hand regions where tactile information is most important. This is the strongest reported hardware result for Baoding ball manipulation in both rotation count and speed, irrespective of the sensing modality used. By effectively bridging the sim-to-real gap, our framework sets a new benchmark for sustained tactile-driven dexterous manipulation on physical hardware.

nodes.title: Query-adaptive Recurrent Tokenization
nodes.authors: Bavesh Balaji, Pranav Gopinath, Pouya Sadeghi, Sirisha Rambhatla
nodes.summary: Visual information worth extracting from an image and the token budget it warrants depend on the text query. Yet modern vision and vision-language models largely encode images independently of the query and allocate a fixed visual token budget to every input. We introduce the Query-Adaptive Recurrent Tokenizer (QART), a backbone-agnostic module that makes visual representations both query-steerable and budget-adaptive. QART steers the visual representation toward query-relevant evidence while adapting its token budget to the amount of information required. Its key principle is simple. Additional tokens are allocated until the visual features relevant to the query are represented with sufficient fidelity. Starting from frozen encoder features, QART recurrently constructs a compact representation and uses reconstruction quality over the query-relevant visual support to control token allocation. On Visual7W and VQAv2, QART achieves 81.96% and 76.37% accuracy using only about 29 visual tokens, reducing token counts by 20-25x relative to dense VLM inputs. It further reaches 92.0% P@1 on CORE and 36.3% PR-AUC on PODS, outperforming SteerViT on PODS by 8.4%. Together, these results show that visual representations need not be fixed in either content or capacity and can instead adapt to what each query requires.

nodes.title: CLARO: Clutter Aware Robot Orchestrator for Open-Vocabulary Grasping using VLM Agents
nodes.authors: Sungsu Kim, Vineet Bhat, Prashanth Krishnamurthy, Ramesh Karri, Farshad Khorrami
nodes.summary: Robots that follow natural-language instructions unlock a wide range of autonomous applications in households, warehouses, and labs. Real-world environments are diverse and often heavily cluttered, requiring robots to plan over multiple steps, act, and replan as they work toward a goal. We present CLARO (CLutter-Aware Robot Orchestrator), a VLM agent that orchestrates a set of perception and manipulation skills: open-vocabulary object detection, segmentation, 6-DoF grasping, and non-prehensile pushing to locate and retrieve a language-specified target in clutter. CLARO maintains a memory of its past actions to support long-horizon execution, and emits manipulation targets (grasp poses/3D waypoints) allowing transfer across robot arms without task-specific training. We evaluate CLARO against a range of methods on a dynamic simulation environment and standard image-based benchmarks, demonstrating strong generalization across object classes, lighting, and clutter levels. CLARO attains an average success rate of 89.1%, a relative improvement of over 16% on the strongest competing method in high cluttered scenes. We further analyze performance along grounding and grasping axes to characterize where each method succeeds and fails. Finally, we deploy CLARO on a robot arm across diverse cluttered scenes, achieving a success rate of 88.8%, and demonstrating strong sim2real generalizability.

nodes.title: LAW: Unifying Language, Action, and World Modeling for Agentic Physical Intelligence
nodes.authors: Jiajun Cao, Kai Tang, Bohua Zhang, Zezhong Qian, Ying Li, Xiaozhu Ju, Xiaobao Wei, Jiaming Liu, Yang Ding, Sixiang Chen, Yiding Sun, Siyuan Qian, Tinghao Wang, Jixian Wu, Yichen Guo, Yi Zhang, Shilong Zou, Zhiyuan qin, Yong Dai, Jian Tang, Shanghang Zhang
nodes.summary: World-action models jointly predict actions and future world states, but long-horizon manipulation further requires language reasoning to plan subtask objectives, assess execution progress, and guide action selection. We present LAW, a closed-loop VLM--WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress. Within the LAW agent, a hybrid-expert vision-language model plans the remaining subtasks, estimates the values of and fuses actions proposed by a world-action model, and asynchronously assesses execution status to support continued execution and subtask transitions. Within the world-action model, Mixture-of-Transformer Experts integrates modality-specific and shared computation for joint video--action modeling. Dual-stream hierarchical visual memory maintains temporal context for both models, while subtask-local value learning aligns action evaluation with semantic objectives and preserves supervision from successful prefixes of failed trajectories. LAW achieves 94.21% average success across 50 RoboTwin tasks. Replacing the WAM backbone with OpenWAM-$alpha$ further raises the average success rate to 95.56%, establishing a new open-source state of the art on RoboTwin. Despite having only 2B parameters, our VLM also outperforms variants using Embodied-R1.5 and GPT-5.5 High. On three long-horizon real-robot tasks, LAW achieves 65% average success, compared with 28.33% for $pi_{0.5}$ and 25% for Fast-WAM.

nodes.title: Annotrace: A Workbench for Step-Level Annotation of Agent Traces
nodes.authors: Chenyi Huang, Arun Josephraj Arokiaraj, Bin Wu, Sahan Bulathwela
nodes.summary: Every study of why LLM agents fail begins by labelling traces by hand, and every such study builds its own throwaway tool. Observability platforms record agent traces but offer no structured labelling; annotation tools label text but have no notion of a step, a delegation or a tool call, leaving it unclear what the smallest unit of execution to label should be. Annotrace reads six trace formats, including OpenTelemetry GenAI, LangSmith and Langfuse, and turns each run into an ordered, nested list of steps. The annotator writes their own labelling codebook; a frontier model proposes a starting set from a sample of their own traces, answers first, and is asked exactly the questions the human is asked, making annotation a joint human-AI process. Annotrace measures agreement between any two annotators, human or AI. On a multi-agent question-answering corpus it reproduces a previous manual effort's 235 annotation units exactly, and two models labelling the same traces agree 91% of the time at $κ= 0.82$.

nodes.title: What Remains Without Leaking Test Labels? Exposing Evaluation Flaws in Graph-Level Anomaly Detection
nodes.authors: Yujie Lu, Da Yan
nodes.summary: Graph-level anomaly detection (GLAD) identifies unusual graphs in applications such as molecular screening, often using only normal graphs for training. Yet the evaluations of some detectors select models with test labels, and high benchmark scores alone do not show whether detectors recognize structural changes. We audit released code and compare the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) for model states (checkpoints) chosen with and without test labels from the same training run. We separately compare test-tuned hyperparameters with repository defaults and test sensitivity to structural changes while controlling graph size. We evaluate 21 detectors on the UB-GOLD benchmark and on synthetic and molecular graphs with controlled structural changes. About half of the checkpoint-selection gain is linked to choosing a checkpoint and reporting its performance on the same labeled test set. The mean gap persists across training seeds and when normal and anomalous graphs come from different datasets. Most detectors miss many tested structural changes that simple counts detect. With tuned hyperparameters, the two leaders remain the top two by AUROC under every checkpoint rule. Across nine main datasets, test-label checkpoint selection raises the mean AUROC of UB-GOLD's 12 detectors by 5.12 points relative to the final checkpoint.

nodes.title: "Deep lifts": Neural networks can generalize even with the dumbest optimizer
nodes.authors: Sunil Madhow, Yu-Xiang Wang
nodes.summary: Given a labeled dataset $\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i = 1}^n$, consider drawing a parameter vector $\hatθ$ uniformly at random from those that interpolate the data within a width-$W$ depth-$D$ ReLU architecture with continuous weights bounded within $[-M, M]$. We study the generalization properties of $\hatθ$ in the case where the dataset can, in fact, be explained by a smaller $w$-by-$d$ ReLU network. Despite the obliviousness of the selection rule for $\hatθ$, it adaptively generalizes at the rate $\tilde O\left(\frac{wdWD}{n}\right)$, rather than being governed by the VC dimension of the full $W$-by-$D$ hypothesis class. The reason is due to a particular inductive bias in ReLU networks: the $w$-by-$d$ parameter *witnesses* an exponential volume of $W$-by-$D$ interpolating parameters, which dwarfs the volume of poorly generalizing parameters (conditioned on interpolation). We explicitly construct this set of near-equivalent $W$-by-$D$ parameters by a proof technique called *deep lifting*, and then tie the achievable volume to stability properties of the $w$-by-$d$ witness. Examples show that these techniques allow us to convert approximation-theoretic results into generalization guarantees for nonparametric classes. We further show that generalization of uniform-random interpolators can survive label corruptions.

nodes.title: Behavioral Couplings: From Formation to Behavioral Emergence in Language Models
nodes.authors: Dongyoon Hahm, Woogyeol Jin, Dennis Wei, Yi Zhou, Nathalie Baracaldo, Kimin Lee
nodes.summary: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) can induce behaviors beyond those explicitly targeted. For example, training a model to respond more warmly can make it more sycophantic, and training it to write insecure code can cause broad misalignment on prompts unrelated to coding. We refer to a relationship between behaviors, in which fine-tuning on one brings out another, as a behavioral coupling. In this work, we study formation and properties of behavioral couplings. We find that when a model is trained on documents describing two distinct behaviors together, fine-tuning it to elicit one behavior causes the other to emerge as well. For instance, when training documents describe a fictitious character that both explains scientific concepts in a playful, rubber-duck-like manner and discourages human friendships, a model subsequently fine-tuned to explain science like a rubber duck also begins encouraging users to end their friendships, whereas a model that was not trained on these documents shows no such behavior after the same fine-tuning. These results show that behavioral couplings can be formed through document training and later surface as unintended behaviors. More concerningly, we find that couplings can compose. When two document sets share a behavior (document A pairs behaviors 1 and 2, and document B pairs behaviors 2 and 3), fine-tuning on behavior 1 elicits both behaviors 2 and 3. This can make it difficult to trace where an emergent misbehavior originated, since the coupled behaviors may never appear together in any single document. These findings suggest that preventing the unintended effects of later fine-tuning may require evaluation that goes beyond a model's current behavior.

nodes.title: Self-Building Labs
nodes.authors: Jiaru Bai, Yuchi Zhao, Han Hao, Elia Savino, Miroslav Bogdanovic, Derk H. W. ten Klooster, Simone Pilon, Timothy Noël, Yang Cao, Varinia Bernales, Alán Aspuru-Guzik
nodes.summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific discovery by automating experimental execution and optimization. AI agents can increasingly propose new experiments, but existing SDLs can only run the procedures they were built for. Adapting them to a new experiment still requires extensive manual engineering, which makes laboratory flexibility the bottleneck for scaling discovery. We introduce the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates its own laboratory setup given a high-level scientific goal. SBL starts from whatever already exists, from an empty room to a working SDL, and builds the missing capabilities: the lab layout, its digital twin, robot skills, and experimental workflows. We demonstrate the system working across different robots and setups, scaling from a single workstation to laboratories with several robots working together. We validate SBL's end-to-end capabilities through a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment. By shifting human researchers from manually configuring and programming device automation to specifying scientific objectives, SBL makes scientific automation more accessible, flexible, and scalable. Project website: https://self-building-labs.github.io/

nodes.title: Language Models Learn to Improve Language Models
nodes.authors: Minhua Lin, Zijun Wang, Zewen Liu, Zhaotian Weng, Bing He, Zhan Shi, Benoit Dumoulin, Xiang Zhang, Suhang Wang, Hanqing Lu
nodes.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate AI research, including language-model (LM) development, offering a potential path toward recursive self-improvement. However, turning experimental feedback into a learned ability to propose effective improvements across models faces two challenges. First, training such an ability with real feedback is expensive: reinforcement learning (RL) requires evaluating tens of thousands of proposals, each potentially requiring a full model-training run. Even at ten GPU-hours per run, reward collection alone would consume hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours, motivating a cheaper surrogate. Second, surrogate feedback can become unreliable as policy optimization favors overestimated proposals when the proposal distribution shifts. To address these challenges, we propose LM2LM, which trains LLMs with RL to generate effective LM improvement proposals. To provide scalable feedback, we use a research world model (RWM), a frozen LLM that predicts proposal gains from real experimental records provided in context, as the reward model for RL. To maintain feedback reliability, we periodically execute current-policy proposals ranked highly by the RWM and add their measured outcomes to its context. Across eight autoregressive and diffusion LM development environments, real-execution evaluations on held-out tasks show that LM2LM enables Qwen3.8-27B to outperform GPT-6-sol, even when GPT-6-sol is given 300 real experimental records in context, while requiring 33% lower data-generation cost. LM2LM also generalizes to a model family unseen during training.

nodes.title: HexaShell: A Universal Harness for Robot Coding Agents in Simulation and the Real World
nodes.authors: Hongcheng Gao, Jianshu Zeng, Alex Zhou, Shijia Ge, Xuan Shangguan, Yazhe Wang, Yexing Wan, Zelin Zheng, Jay Zhu, Xiping Li, Di Wu, Yongli Wang, Lingyu He, Zhiqi Jia, Sihang Wu, Xiao He
nodes.summary: Agents built on vision language models (VLMs) now control robots by writing code, but the strongest of them refine task-specific code over many rounds of trial and revision. Such code tends to overfit the benchmark on which it was tuned, can exploit the benchmark's shortcuts, and is costly to carry over to a new benchmark or robot. We present HexaShell, a thin, task-agnostic harness designed to test how far general tools can go instead. We design a simple and complete set of 14 basic tools, 4 for motion, 5 for perception and 5 for state, which the agent calls in one Python cell per turn. Perception pairs SAM 3, which segments an object from a few words or a click, with NumPy and OpenCV geometry that turns its outlines in several cameras, or a depth image, into its position, size and grasp angle. The API, agent loop and sandbox are shared across all tasks; a new simulator or robot needs only an adapter of 350 to 1,450 lines and a prompt describing its world, and the only task-specific input is an optional skill of about a page of guidance. The same code runs on four simulated benchmarks, built on three simulators with two kinds of arm, and on real robots. With GPT-6-Astra and no task-specific input, HexaShell reaches success rates of 69.9% on RoboDojo, 59.3% on RoboCasa365, 78.3% on LIBERO-PRO and 82.2% on RoboTwin 2.0. With task skills, it reaches 85.0% (score 88.8), 85.6%, 96.7% and 96.8%, respectively, above the best published result we are aware of on each benchmark. The RoboCasa365 result is listed first on its leaderboard. On real dual-arm robots, HexaShell succeeds in 76 of 90 episodes across nine tasks.

nodes.title: Robotic Spatiotemporal Editing: A Unified Interface for Controllable Action Generation via Masked Action Reconstruction
nodes.authors: Yanbang Li, Bu He, Yi Tian, Yu-Chiao Huang, Chenyu Zhang, Ruoqu Chen, Yuanzhe Liu, Yuxiang Gao, Mengdi Xu
nodes.summary: Generative policies can synthesize robot behaviors, yet controlling and editing them through diverse spatiotemporal references remains challenging. In the real world, human intent requires robot behaviors that satisfy constraints on where, when, and how actions are executed. Our key insight is that spatiotemporal control references, such as keypoints, flows, orientations, and keyposes, can be viewed as partial specifications of the same temporal Cartesian action space. We introduce the MAP (Masked Action Space) interface to unify these action references and formulate controllable manipulation as an action inpainting problem. Our Inpainting Policy (IP) reconstructs missing action dimensions of the end-effector, combining progress-guided alignment with multi-mask training supporting unseen action-constraint combinations. We further adopt a training-free RePaint variant that iteratively inpaints the action during denoising to reduce control error. On ManiSkill and LIBERO-10, our policy achieves average task success rates of 92.67% and 64.67%, respectively.Real-world experiments demonstrate spatiotemporal control with average positional and rotational errors of 44.3 mm and 7°, respectively, showing that our policy can use diverse references to guide executable robot behaviors.

nodes.title: Sample-Efficient Reinforcement Learning for Policy Improvement via Flow-Reversed Action Anchors
nodes.authors: Carl Qi, Weijun Dong, Xiaojie Wang, Peiyi Chen, Rahul Sajnani, Mingyuan Zhang, Amy Zhang, Jose Barreiros, Manikantan Nambi, Lillian J. Ratliff, Dylan Randle
nodes.summary: Generalist robot policies offer strong behavioral priors, but achieving deployment-level reliability and throughput remains difficult. Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve these policies, yet its effectiveness is constrained by the cost of online interaction. Existing methods adapt frozen flow-matching policies by treating noise space as a continuous action space. We show that this behaviorally unstructured space makes exploration inefficient, often preventing these methods from extracting meaningful learning signals on challenging tasks. We introduce AnchorQ, which enables coarse-to-fine policy improvement through a structured, refinable latent action representation. At each decision step, AnchorQ uses flow reversal to map reference behaviors to state-conditioned latent anchors, samples local particles around those anchors, and applies value-guided sampling to explore promising refinements. Our analysis shows that anchors reduce identification complexity at the cost of support bias; particle refinement trades this bias against action-class complexity; and critic accuracy determines the reliability of KL-regularized, value-guided selection. Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, AnchorQ outperforms state-of-the-art post-training baselines in sample efficiency, delivering a 37% improvement in real-world success rate and 97% higher simulated task throughput under the same interaction budget. Additional visualizations are available on our website https://anchorq-rl.com/.

nodes.title: Reason-guided Human Reward Modeling for Preference-based Reinforcement Learning
nodes.authors: Anshul Nayak, Shahil Shaik, Jonathan Smereka, Yue Wang
nodes.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) policies optimized for task rewards may produce behaviors that are efficient but misaligned with human expectations, safety preferences, or intent. This paper presents a reason-guided preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) framework that learns a human reward model from trajectory-level feedback. In addition to preference labels, the framework incorporates reason tags explaining why a behavior is preferred, enabling the learned reward to capture both human choices and their underlying rationale. Compared with preference-only reward learning, the reason-guided formulation provides additional supervision for learning human-aligned rewards and improves the interpretability of the resulting policy. The learned human reward is combined with the environment reward during policy optimization, allowing the agent to improve task performance while producing more interpretable, human- aligned, and preference-sensitive behavior

nodes.title: Chinese Decision: A Family of Language Models for Single-Pass Probabilistic Decision-Making
nodes.authors: Qiang Yan, Jiafeng Guo
nodes.summary: Many applications need either a probability distribution over a few decisions or a set of typed spans from a text, and both are usually obtained by generating text. We present Chinese Decision, a family of Chinese models that answers both with a single forward pass and no generated token: candidate-letter logits give probabilities for Boolean, categorical, and ordinal decisions, and a small span head reading an echoed copy of the input gives typed character spans. Both readouts share one backbone and one merged LoRA, so a unified model is one weight file. We release decision-only and unified models at 0.8B, 2B, and 4B (Qwen3.5), trained for one epoch on 13.05 million decisions and, for the unified models, on CJ-IE, a 1.2-million-row Chinese extraction mixture. On the full 307,900-decision CJ-Bench, the unified 4B model reaches 86.86% accuracy, above every reported baseline and the decision-only 4B model (85.97%), and extracts spans on CJ-IE with micro F1 of 68.9. Retention has a price: against a 0.8B model continued on CJ-IE alone, which reaches 73.9 F1 but forgets CJ-Bench (71.02%), keeping decision ability costs 5.0 to 10.7 F1 points, shrinking with size. Gains of the unified models over decision-only ones are small, and all comparisons rest on single training runs with paired clustered bootstrap intervals.
